one: An API style where URLs name resources (nouns) and HTTP methods say what to do with them.
an: A library catalogue: every book has an address (/books/42), and a small set of verbs works on every address the same way.
how: Resources: GET /orders, GET /orders/42, POST /orders, PATCH /orders/42, DELETE /orders/42. Nested where it reads naturally: /orders/42/items.
Leans on HTTP itself: status codes for outcomes, headers for caching (ETag), content negotiation, auth.
Usually described with an OpenAPI spec, which can generate docs, client SDKs and validation.
why: It is the default because every language, proxy, cache and browser already speaks it. Simple to cache at the HTTP layer.
trade: Over-fetching (endpoint returns more than the screen needs) and under-fetching (a screen needs 5 calls). Actions that are not CRUD (POST /orders/42/refund) are fine; do not contort them into fake resources.

myth.r: Most are "REST-ish". Strict REST (HATEOAS, hypermedia links) is rare in practice. What matters is consistency.

q.s: A mobile screen needs a user, their last 5 orders and each order's items: 7 REST calls on a slow network. Which option does NOT address this?
o: A purpose-built endpoint for that screen (backend-for-frontend)
GraphQL
An include parameter like ?include=orders.items
Adding more status codes
q.e: The problem is round trips. A BFF endpoint, GraphQL, or include/expand parameters all collapse them. Status codes are unrelated.

more: Consistent error format across endpoints
Filtering, sorting and sparse fieldsets conventions
Long-running operations: 202 Accepted + status resource
Bulk endpoints and partial failures
OpenAPI: spec-first vs code-first and generating clients
lab: Design (on paper) a REST API for a car-wash booking app: resources, methods, status codes, error format.
Implement two endpoints with Fastify or Express and generate an OpenAPI spec from them (e.g. @fastify/swagger).
Generate a typed TS client from the spec with openapi-typescript and call it from a React page.
Compare your design with one public API you admire (Stripe, GitHub).

plain:
REST is a common way to design an API. You think in resources (things: orders, users, products), give each a URL, and use HTTP methods as the verbs: GET to read, POST to create, PATCH to change, DELETE to remove.

Because it uses plain HTTP, every tool already understands it: browsers, caches, proxies, monitoring.
bridge: Most APIs you have consumed with fetch are REST-style. Designing them yourself means deciding the URLs, status codes and error format that frontend developers like you will rely on.

walk.title: Designing the API for a booking app
steps: Resources: /venues, /venues/:id/slots, /bookings.
List: GET /venues?city=Tashkent&limit=20 → 200 with a page of venues and a cursor for the next page.
Create: POST /bookings with {slotId} → 201 with the booking. If the slot is taken → 409 Conflict.
Cancel: not really a delete (you keep history), so POST /bookings/:id/cancel → 200. Actions like this are fine in REST.
Every error uses the same shape, the standard application/problem+json: { type, title, status: 409, detail, code: 'slot_taken' }. The frontend handles errors in one place.

terms: A thing your API exposes, with its own URL.
A standard file format that describes an API; tools generate docs and clients from it.
Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same result as once.
insights: Consistency matters more than purity. A predictable API is easier to use than a “perfectly RESTful” one.
Generate TypeScript types from the OpenAPI spec so the frontend breaks at compile time, not in production, when the API changes.

prod.summary: In production, a REST API is a contract that many clients depend on for years. Seniors care less about “pure REST” and more about consistency: the same error shape everywhere, correct status codes, pagination on every list, an OpenAPI spec that matches the real behaviour, and limits on everything a client can ask for.
checklist: Every error uses one format. application/problem+json (RFC 9457) is the standard choice: type, title, status, detail, plus your own machine-readable code.

Status codes mean what they say: 201 + Location on create, 400 for bad syntax, 422 for valid JSON that fails business validation, 404 vs 403 chosen on purpose, 409 for conflicts, 429 for limits. Never 200 with { success: false }.
Every list endpoint is paginated with a maximum limit enforced on the server, even if today the table is small.
Request bodies are validated against a schema (Zod, TypeBox, JSON Schema) and unknown fields are either rejected or ignored on purpose, not by accident.
The OpenAPI spec is checked in CI against the real routes (generated from code, or contract-tested), and breaking changes are detected with a diff tool such as oasdiff.
POST endpoints with side effects (payments, orders) accept an Idempotency-Key so client retries are safe.
Responses never leak internals: no stack traces, no SQL error text, no internal hostnames in 500 bodies. A request ID goes into the response and the logs instead.
numbers: GitHub REST API: 5,000 requests per hour for an authenticated user; list endpoints use per_page (max 100) and a Link header for the next page.
Stripe API: global limit of 100 requests per second per account in live mode, 25 in sandbox; above that you get 429.
RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE as idempotent. POST and PATCH are not idempotent by definition.
failures: Frontend shows “Something went wrong” for every error, and support tickets cannot be triaged.

Each endpoint returns errors in a different shape, so the client can only show a generic message. Fix: one error middleware that maps every thrown error to problem+json with a stable code field, and a request ID the user can quote.
Monitoring shows 0% errors, but users report failures.
The API returns 200 with { ok: false } on failure. Dashboards, retries and caches all treat it as success. Fix: return real 4xx/5xx codes; alert on the 5xx rate per route.
Database CPU jumps to 100% when one client calls GET /orders?limit=100000.
No server-side maximum for limit. Fix: clamp it (for example to 100), and paginate with cursors for deep lists.
Generated TypeScript client compiles, but crashes at runtime on a field that is null.

The OpenAPI spec says the field is required and non-null, but the code sometimes returns null. The spec drifted from reality. Fix: generate the spec from the route schemas, or validate responses against the spec in tests.

code.title: Fastify route: 201 + Location, 409 conflict, problem+json errors
code.note: The error handler is the important part: every route gets the same error shape for free, and 5xx responses never expose the real error message. Fastify 5 types the handler's err as unknown, so <FastifyError> declares what you expect. With Fastify's default settings, additionalProperties: false silently removes unknown fields instead of rejecting them; set ajv.customOptions.removeAdditional: false if you want a 400.

qs.s: A client sends POST /bookings with valid JSON, but the requested date is in the past. Which response fits best?
o: 422 with a problem+json body explaining the field
400 with an HTML error page
200 with { success: false }
500, because the server could not create the booking
qs.e: The request is well-formed but breaks a business rule, which is what 422 (Unprocessable Content) describes. Many APIs also use 400 for this, which is acceptable, but an HTML page breaks clients. 200 hides the failure from monitoring, and 5xx means the server is at fault, which would trigger alerts and client retries.

qs.s: Your list endpoint returns { items: [...] } with no pagination. The table has 300 rows today. A teammate says pagination can wait. What is the strongest reason to add it now?
o: Paginated endpoints are faster for 300 rows
REST requires pagination on every collection
Adding pagination later changes the response contract, and old clients will still expect the full list
Browsers cannot parse JSON arrays longer than 1,000 items
qs.e: Once mobile apps assume “one call returns everything”, introducing pages is a breaking change you must version around. For 300 rows there is no speed benefit, and REST has no such rule. Adding a limit and nextCursor from day one costs almost nothing.

qs.s: Logs show many 500 responses from PATCH /users/:id. The cause is a unique constraint error from Postgres when two users pick the same username. What should the API return instead?
o: 500 is correct because the database threw
404, because the username was not found
429, so the client retries later
409 Conflict with a code like username_taken
qs.e: This is a predictable conflict with the current state, not a server bug, so 409 fits. Returning 500 makes alerts fire for normal user behaviour and tells clients to retry, which will fail again. Catch the constraint error (Postgres code 23505) and map it.

qs.s: Read this traffic. The client retries when !res.ok, and the dashboard alerts on the 4xx/5xx rate. What goes wrong?

code.title: POST /orders

o: Nothing. The body explains the error, and every client should read the body before the status.
It should return 500, so the client retries until stock comes back.
res.ok is true, so the client and the dashboards count this as a success. Return a 4xx (for example 409) with a problem+json body.
It should return 404, because the item cannot be delivered.
qs.e: Status codes are what generic tools read: fetch, retry logic, caches, load balancers and dashboards. A 200 with success:false is invisible to all of them. 500 is tempting but wrong: out of stock is not a server bug, and retrying will not fix it. 409 (conflict with current state) or 422 with a stable code like out_of_stock lets the client show the right message.

qs.s: A mobile app sends PUT /users/42 with body {"name":"Aziza"} to change only the name. Read the handler. What happens to the user's phone and city?

code.title: users.ts

o: They are set to NULL. PUT means “replace the whole resource”, and this handler does exactly that. Partial changes should use PATCH and update only the fields that were sent.
Nothing changes for phone and city, because missing JSON fields are ignored.
Postgres rejects the query, because parameters cannot be NULL.
The request fails with 400, because HTTP requires PUT bodies to contain every field.
qs.e: The code writes null for every field the client did not send, so data is lost. That is correct PUT semantics (full replacement), but the client wanted a partial update. The tempting answer “missing fields are ignored” is only true if the handler is written that way; nothing in HTTP or JSON does it for you. Use PATCH and build the SET list from the fields that are present.

qs.s: Two admins open product 7 at the same time. Admin A changes the price, admin B changes the description. Both send PATCH /products/7 with the full form. B's request arrives last and silently overwrites A's new price. Which REST mechanism prevents this “lost update”?
o: Return 409 Conflict on every PATCH.
Send Cache-Control: no-store on the GET.
Require an Idempotency-Key on PATCH.
Return an ETag on GET; clients send If-Match with it on PATCH; the server answers 412 Precondition Failed if the product changed since that version.
qs.e: Conditional requests (optimistic concurrency) detect that the resource changed after the client read it. B gets 412, reloads, and merges. An Idempotency-Key is tempting but solves a different problem: it stops the same request from running twice, not two different requests from overwriting each other. Sending only changed fields in PATCH also reduces the damage, but two edits to the same field still collide.

qs.s: User A (tenant 1) calls GET /invoices/981. Invoice 981 exists but belongs to tenant 2. Which response is the safer default?
o: 403 Forbidden, because the user is logged in but not allowed.
404 Not Found, so the API does not confirm that invoice 981 exists in another tenant.
401 Unauthorized, so the client logs in again.
200 with an empty body.
qs.e: 403 tells an attacker “this ID exists, you just cannot see it”, which helps them enumerate other customers' data. Returning 404 for resources outside the caller's tenant is what GitHub does for private repositories. 403 is still right when the user can know the resource exists (for example, a read-only member trying to delete a project they can see). 401 means “not authenticated”, which is not the case here.

interview.q: How would you design error responses for a public REST API?
answer: One format for every endpoint, ideally application/problem+json (RFC 9457): type, title, status, detail.
A stable, machine-readable code (for example slot_taken) that clients branch on. Messages can change; codes cannot.
Correct status codes so generic tools work: 400/422 for input, 401 vs 403 vs 404 chosen on purpose, 409 for state conflicts, 429 with Retry-After, 5xx only for server faults.
Validation errors list every bad field with a path (items[2].qty), so a form can show all errors at once.
A request ID in every response and in the logs; never stack traces, SQL text or hostnames in the body.
The error format and codes are part of the OpenAPI contract and are covered by the same breaking-change checks as successful responses.
followups: Would you ever return 200 with an error inside?
How do you localise error messages?
How do clients know which errors are safe to retry?

interview.q: When do you use POST, PUT and PATCH, and what does idempotency have to do with the choice?
answer: POST creates or triggers an action; the server picks the ID. It is not idempotent, so side-effecting POSTs need an Idempotency-Key to be retried safely.
PUT replaces the whole resource at a URL the client knows. It is idempotent by definition (RFC 9110), so clients and proxies may retry it.
PATCH changes part of a resource. It is not idempotent in general ({op: "increment"}), but “set these fields to these values” is idempotent in practice.
Actions that are not CRUD (POST /orders/42/refund) are fine; do not invent fake resources to avoid them.
Concurrent edits need ETag + If-Match (412 on mismatch) whichever method you use.
followups: How would you design an “increment quantity” endpoint so retries are safe?
What is the difference between a safe and an idempotent method?

interview.q: How do you keep API documentation correct as the API changes?
answer: Single source of truth: either spec-first (OpenAPI file, code generated or validated against it) or code-first (spec generated from route schemas). Never a hand-written spec next to unrelated code.
Route schemas validate requests at runtime, so the spec cannot claim one thing while the code accepts another.
Tests validate real responses against the spec, which catches drift such as a field that is sometimes null.
CI runs a breaking-change diff (oasdiff) on every PR and blocks unannounced breaks.
Typed clients are generated from the spec, so frontend code fails at compile time when the contract changes.
followups: Spec-first or code-first: which do you prefer and why?
How do you document error responses?

videos.t: Deep Dive into REST API Design and Implementation Best Practices
videos.why: Naming, status codes and resource modelling best practices.

one: One endpoint where the client sends a query describing exactly which fields it wants, and gets back that shape.
an: Ordering à la carte instead of fixed set menus. The client writes the order; the kitchen (resolvers) fetches each item.
how: A typed schema defines types and fields. Clients send queries (read), mutations (write) and subscriptions (live).
Each field has a resolver function on the server. The engine walks the query and calls resolvers to assemble the response.
Tooling generates TypeScript types from the schema, so the frontend is type-safe end to end.
why: Many different clients (web, iOS, Android) need different slices of the same data. GraphQL lets them ask for exactly that without new endpoints.
trade: Naive resolvers cause N+1 database queries (solved with DataLoader batching). HTTP caching is harder: most clients send every operation as a POST to one URL, so CDNs cannot cache by URL unless you use GET for queries with persisted queries. Clients can send expensive deeply nested queries, so you need depth/complexity limits or a persisted-query allowlist.

myth.r: It is an API layer. Resolvers can read from SQL, other services, anywhere.

q.s: A query for 50 posts with their authors makes 51 SQL queries. What is the standard fix?
o: Switch to REST
Batch author lookups per request with a DataLoader
Add a CDN
Increase DB connections
q.e: DataLoader collects all author IDs requested in one tick and runs one WHERE id IN (...) query.

more: Fragments and colocating data needs with components (Relay, Apollo)
Normalised client caches and cache updates after mutations
Persisted queries and query cost analysis
Federation: one graph across many services
Errors in GraphQL: partial data with an errors array, HTTP 200
lab: Build a small schema (User, Post) with GraphQL Yoga or Apollo Server.
Log SQL queries and run a query for 20 posts with authors. Count the queries (N+1).
Add DataLoader and count again.
Write a deeply nested malicious query and add a depth limit that rejects it.

plain:
With GraphQL there is one endpoint. The client sends a query describing exactly which fields it wants, possibly across related data, and gets back JSON in that exact shape.

On the server, each field has a small function (a resolver) that knows how to get it.
bridge: Instead of calling /users/1, then /users/1/orders, then /products/... and combining them in a useEffect, you write one query that mirrors your component tree and get everything at once.

walk.title: One profile page, one request
steps: The query: { user(id: 1) { name avatar orders(last: 5) { total items { product { title } } } } }.
The server's resolvers: user loads the user, orders loads 5 orders, items loads items, product loads each product.
Naively, loading the product for each item is one SQL query per item: the N+1 problem.
With DataLoader, all product IDs requested in that moment are collected and loaded in one WHERE id IN (...) query.
The client receives exactly the fields it asked for, nothing more.

terms: The typed description of everything the API offers.
A server function that produces one field's value.
A helper that batches many small lookups into one.
insights: GraphQL moves complexity from the client to the server. It is worth it when many different clients need different data.
Design the schema around what screens need, not around database tables. A schema that copies your tables gives you REST's problems with a new syntax.

prod.summary: In production, the hard parts of GraphQL are not the schema but the server: N+1 queries hidden in resolvers, queries that cost 1,000× more than others, errors that come back with HTTP 200, and caching. Seniors put cost limits in front of the resolvers, a DataLoader per request behind them, and per-operation metrics, because the URL alone tells monitoring nothing.
checklist: DataLoaders are created per request (in the context factory), never as module-level singletons, or one user's cached data leaks into another user's response.
Query depth and cost limits are enforced, and list fields require a first/limit argument with a maximum. For first-party apps, consider a persisted-query allowlist so only known operations run.
Metrics and traces are tagged by operation name and resolver, not by URL. Every request goes to /graphql, so URL-based dashboards are useless.

Error handling is designed: partial data plus an errors array is normal. Clients check errors, and expected business errors are modelled as typed results (for example a union with an error type) instead of exceptions.
Introspection and detailed error messages are turned off or restricted for public production endpoints if the schema is not meant to be public.
CSRF protection is on: Apollo Server enables csrfPrevention by default, which blocks simple cross-site GET/POST requests without a custom header.
Schema changes are checked in CI against real client operations (schema registry or graphql-inspector), because removing a field breaks old mobile apps exactly like in REST.
numbers: GitHub GraphQL API: every connection needs first or last between 1 and 100, and one call may request at most 500,000 total nodes.
GitHub GraphQL API rate limit is calculated in points (query cost), not in request count: 5,000 points per hour for a user.
DataLoader batches all load() calls made in the same tick of the event loop into one batchLoadFn call.
failures: A dashboard query takes 4 seconds; the DB log shows hundreds of identical SELECT ... WHERE id = $1 queries.
Classic N+1: a field resolver loads one row per parent item. Fix: a DataLoader per request that batches IDs into one WHERE id = ANY($1) query, and return results in the same order as the keys.
User A sees user B's private data after a deploy.
A DataLoader (or another cache) was created at module level, so its cache lived across requests and users. Fix: build loaders in the per-request context function.
The API is down after one client sends a query nested 15 levels deep (friends { friends { friends ... } }).
No depth or cost limits. Fix: add a depth limit and a cost analysis plugin, require pagination arguments on lists, and use persisted queries for your own apps.
Error rate on the dashboard is 0%, but the mobile app shows empty screens.
GraphQL returns HTTP 200 with an errors array for resolver errors, so HTTP-based monitoring sees success. Fix: record GraphQL errors as a metric per operation and alert on them.

code.title: DataLoader created per request to batch author lookups
code.note: Fifty Post.author resolvers now produce one SQL query. The order of the returned array must match ids, or authors get attached to the wrong posts.

qs.s: Your public GraphQL API has a CDN in front of it, but the cache hit rate is 0%. Clients send queries with POST /graphql. Which change makes CDN caching possible?
o: Add Cache-Control headers to the POST responses
Switch the database to a read replica
Turn on HTTP/2
Send queries as GET with persisted query hashes, and set cache headers per operation
qs.e: CDNs cache GET responses by URL; POST responses are not cached by normal CDN rules, so headers alone do not help. Persisted queries keep the GET URL short (a hash plus variables). Read replicas and HTTP/2 do not affect CDN caching.

qs.s: A resolver throws “Not allowed to view salary” for one field. What does the client typically receive?
o: HTTP 403 and no data at all
HTTP 200 with the other fields filled, salary: null, and an entry in errors
HTTP 500 and an HTML error page
HTTP 200 with the field silently missing and no error
qs.e: GraphQL returns partial results: the failing field becomes null (if nullable) and the error is listed in errors with a path. If the field were non-null, the null would spread up to the nearest nullable parent. That is why clients must always check errors, not just the status code.

qs.s: Engineers want to know which part of the API is slow. Every request goes to /graphql. What should the tracing setup record?
o: The operation name and per-resolver timings
Only the HTTP status code
The full query text as the metric label
The client IP address
qs.e: Operation names (query DashboardPage) group requests by meaning, and resolver timings show which field is slow. Status codes are almost always 200. Full query text as a label creates unlimited label values and breaks metric storage (high cardinality).

qs.s: After renameUser succeeds, queries keep returning the old name for that user until the server restarts. Read the code. What is the cause?

code.title: resolvers.ts

o: The database update is not committed before the query runs.
The loader is created once at module level, so its memoization cache lives for the whole process and keeps the old user forever. Create loaders per request in the context.
DataLoader only batches; it never caches, so the problem must be a CDN.
findMany with in returns rows in random order, so the wrong user is returned.
qs.e: DataLoader caches every key it loaded (memoization) for its own lifetime. That is meant to last one request. At module level it becomes a process-wide cache with no invalidation, which serves stale data and can leak one user's data to another. The order answer is tempting, but this code maps results back by ID, so order is handled.

qs.s: Calculate: in the worst case, how many objects (nodes) can this single query return?

code.title: query.graphql

qs.e: Limits multiply down the tree: 50 repositories + 50×20 = 1,000 issues + 1,000×10 = 10,000 labels = 11,050 nodes. That is why GitHub's GraphQL API calculates cost from first/last arguments before running a query. 80 (adding the limits) is the tempting wrong answer: it ignores that each level runs once per parent.

qs.s: Your GraphQL API serves only your own web and mobile apps. Security asks how to stop attackers from sending arbitrary, expensive queries. Which option is the strongest?
o: Trusted documents (a persisted-query allowlist): operations are registered at build time, and the server executes only known operation hashes.
Turn off introspection so attackers cannot see the schema.
Add a depth limit of 10.
Rate limit to 60 requests per minute per IP.
qs.e: If the server only runs operations your apps were built with, an attacker cannot send a new query at all. Turning off introspection is tempting but is obscurity: field names leak from the app bundle and from error suggestions. Depth limits and rate limits help, but one allowed request can still be very expensive (wide lists at depth 3).

qs.s: The team wants to remove the deprecated total field. Mobile app versions from the last 18 months are still installed. What is the safe process?

code.title: schema.graphql

o: Remove it now. @deprecated already told every client to stop using it.
Nothing is needed. GraphQL has no breaking changes, because clients choose their fields.
Use operation usage data (a schema registry or logged operations per client version) to see who still requests total; remove it only when usage is zero or only from unsupported app versions.
Move the whole API to /graphql/v2.
qs.e: A query that asks for a field that no longer exists fails validation, so the whole operation fails, not just that field. Old mobile apps keep sending their old queries. “Clients choose their fields” is the tempting myth: it makes adding fields safe, not removing them. GraphQL's usual answer is continuous evolution with usage tracking, not URL versions.

interview.q: When would you choose GraphQL over REST for a new product, and when would you not?
answer: Good fit: several clients (web, iOS, Android) with different data needs, deeply related data, a frontend team that wants to move without new endpoints.
Poor fit: simple CRUD with one client, public APIs where HTTP caching and curl-friendliness matter, file uploads and streaming-heavy work.
The cost moves to the server: N+1 control with DataLoader, query cost limits, per-operation monitoring, and error handling with HTTP 200.
Caching changes: CDN caching needs GET + persisted queries; clients rely on normalised caches (Apollo, Relay, urql).
Authorization must be enforced per field or per type in resolvers or the business layer, not per URL.
followups: How would you cache GraphQL responses at the edge?
Where do you put authorization checks?

interview.q: How do you protect a public GraphQL API from expensive or malicious queries?
answer: Static cost analysis before execution: assign a cost per field, multiply by list arguments, reject above a budget (GitHub's points model).
Require pagination arguments on every list with a maximum (for example first ≤ 100).
Depth and alias limits, and limits on query size and number of operations per request (batching attacks).
Rate limit by cost points per client, not by request count.
For first-party clients, a persisted-query allowlist; plus server timeouts so a slow resolver cannot hold resources forever.
followups: How would you estimate the cost of a field that calls another service?
What is an alias-based attack?

interview.q: Walk me through solving N+1 in GraphQL and the pitfalls of DataLoader.
answer: N+1 appears because each field resolver runs per parent: 50 posts → 50 author lookups.
DataLoader collects load() calls made in the same tick and calls one batch function with all keys (WHERE id = ANY($1)).
The batch function must return exactly one result per key, in key order; missing rows become null or an Error.
Create loaders per request: a shared loader caches across users (data leaks, stale data after mutations).
Inside one request, clear or prime the loader after a mutation if later resolvers read the changed object.
Loaders batch per type and key shape; nested lists (posts → comments) need a loader keyed by parent ID that returns arrays.
followups: How would you batch a one-to-many relation?
How do you detect N+1 in production?

videos.t: What Is GraphQL? REST vs. GraphQL
videos.why: GraphQL next to REST: what changes and what it costs.

videos.t: tRPC, gRPC, GraphQL or REST: when to use what?
videos.why: When to pick tRPC, gRPC, GraphQL or REST.

one: A fast, typed RPC framework: you define services in a .proto file and call remote functions as if they were local.
an: REST is sending letters in plain language. gRPC is two machines agreeing on a compact codebook first, then exchanging short coded messages.
how: You write a .proto file with messages and service methods. Codegen produces client and server stubs in many languages.
Messages are encoded as Protocol Buffers: binary, small, fast to parse. Transport is HTTP/2, so it supports streaming in both directions.
Fields are numbered; adding new fields stays backward compatible as long as you never reuse a number.
why: Common for service-to-service traffic inside a backend where both sides are yours and speed and strict contracts matter.
trade: Browsers cannot call gRPC directly (need gRPC-Web or a proxy). Binary payloads are harder to debug with curl. Usually REST/GraphQL at the edge, gRPC inside.

myth.r: It shines internally. Public APIs still favour REST/JSON because every client can use them.

q.s: Why would a team choose gRPC between internal services but keep REST for their public API?
o: gRPC cannot do streaming

REST is faster

plain:
gRPC lets one service call a function on another service as if it were local. You describe the functions and messages in a .proto file, and tools generate client and server code in many languages.

Messages are sent in a compact binary format over HTTP/2, so it is fast. It is mostly used between backend services, not from browsers.

steps: Write service Pricing { rpc GetPrice(PriceRequest) returns (PriceReply); } and the message fields with numbers.
Generate code: the Pricing team gets a server stub to fill in; the Checkout team gets a client.
Checkout calls pricing.getPrice({ productId: 7 }) like a normal async function.
Under the hood: binary message over an HTTP/2 connection, with a deadline (e.g. 300ms) so it never hangs forever.

prod.summary: In production, gRPC problems are rarely about Protobuf speed. They are about deadlines that were never set, load balancers that send all traffic to one pod because HTTP/2 connections are long-lived, message size limits, and .proto changes that silently corrupt data. Seniors treat the .proto file as a public contract with lint and breaking-change checks in CI.
checklist: Every client call sets a deadline. gRPC has no default deadline, so a stuck server can make clients wait forever and pile up.
Deadlines are propagated to downstream calls, so work stops when the original caller has already given up.

Load balancing works per request, not per connection: client-side balancing (headless Kubernetes Service + round_robin) or an L7 proxy (Envoy, a service mesh). A plain L4 Service pins each client to one pod.
Removed fields are marked reserved (both number and name) so nobody reuses them; buf breaking runs in CI.
Status codes are chosen on purpose: INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, UNAVAILABLE (safe to retry), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. Retries only for idempotent methods.
Message size is bounded: large results are streamed or paginated instead of one huge message.
Health checking uses the standard grpc.health.v1.Health service so Kubernetes probes and balancers understand it.
numbers: Default maximum received message size in gRPC core is 4 MB (4 * 1024 * 1024 bytes); larger messages fail with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.
Protobuf field numbers 1–15 take one byte to encode; use them for the most frequent fields. Numbers 19,000–19,999 are reserved for the Protobuf implementation.
gRPC does not set a deadline by default; the grpc.io guide says to always set an explicit one.
failures: After scaling the Pricing service from 2 to 10 pods, 2 pods still get almost all the traffic.

Clients opened long-lived HTTP/2 connections to the first pods, and a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service balances connections, not requests. Fix: client-side round_robin over a headless Service, or an L7 proxy/mesh; optionally set max_connection_age on servers so clients reconnect.
Checkout requests hang for minutes during a Pricing outage, and Checkout runs out of memory.
No deadlines, so every call waits forever and requests pile up. Fix: set a deadline on each call (for example 300 ms), propagate it, and fail fast with a fallback.
After a deploy, some orders have wrong prices but no errors are logged.

A developer deleted a field and reused its number for a new field with a different meaning. Old clients decode the new value as the old field. Fix: never reuse numbers; mark them reserved; run buf breaking in CI.
Calls fail with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Received message larger than max.
The response grew past the 4 MB default receive limit. Fix: paginate or use server streaming; raise the limit only deliberately.

code.note: reserved makes the compiler reject any future field that tries to reuse number 3 or the old name. The package name has a version (v1) so a real breaking change can live in v2 side by side.

qs.s: A Go client calls a Node gRPC service. The client sets a 200 ms deadline. The Node handler calls the database, which takes 2 seconds. What happens?
o: The client waits the full 2 seconds, then gets the result
The server automatically cancels the database query
The client gets DEADLINE_EXCEEDED after about 200 ms; the server keeps working unless it checks for cancellation
The call is retried automatically until it succeeds
qs.e: The deadline ends the call on the client side, and the server is told the call was cancelled. But your handler code (and the DB query) keeps running unless you watch the cancellation signal and stop. gRPC does not retry automatically unless a retry policy is configured.

qs.s: You need to change int32 quantity = 5; to string quantity = 5; to support values like “2.5kg”. Old clients are still running. What is the safe approach?
o: Add a new field string quantity_text = 9;, keep field 5, migrate clients, then reserve 5
Change the type in place; Protobuf converts it automatically
Change the type and bump the package to v1.1
Delete field 5 and add the string field with number 5
qs.e: Field number + type is the wire contract. Changing the type of an existing number makes old and new versions decode each other's bytes wrongly. Reusing the number after deleting is the same mistake. Add a new field and expand-migrate-contract.

qs.s: A team exposes gRPC directly to its React app. Which is the realistic option for browser calls?
o: Browsers support gRPC natively over HTTP/2
Use WebSockets with Protobuf, which is what gRPC uses internally
It is impossible; browsers can only call REST
Use gRPC-Web or Connect through a proxy or a server that speaks those protocols
qs.e: Browsers do not give JavaScript the low-level HTTP/2 control (such as trailers) that gRPC needs. gRPC-Web and the Connect protocol work over normal fetch, with an Envoy proxy or a server that supports them. gRPC does not use WebSockets.

qs.s: The Pricing service runs behind this headless Service, and clients use dns:///pricing…:50051 with round_robin. After scaling from 3 to 6 pods, the 3 new pods get almost no traffic for a long time. Why?

code.title: pricing-svc.yaml
code.src:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: pricing
spec:
  clusterIP: None        # headless: DNS returns every pod IP
  selector:
    app: pricing
  ports:
    - name: grpc
      port: 50051
# client: new Client("dns:///pricing.default.svc.cluster.local:50051", creds,
#   { "grpc.service_config": '{"loadBalancingConfig":[{"round_robin":{}}]}' })

o: Clients resolved DNS when they connected and keep their existing connections; they re-resolve mainly when a connection breaks. Set max_connection_age on the servers so clients reconnect and pick up new pods.
Headless Services do not work with gRPC; use a normal ClusterIP Service.
round_robin balances connections, not requests.
Kubernetes must restart client pods to update their iptables rules.
qs.e: The client-side balancer only knows the addresses it resolved. Long-lived HTTP/2 connections never break on their own, so new pods stay unknown. Server-side max_connection_age (plus a grace period) forces periodic reconnects and re-resolution. A plain ClusterIP Service is the tempting answer, but it is worse: kube-proxy balances per connection, so each client sticks to one pod.

qs.s: Checkout's caller set a 300 ms deadline on placeOrder. Read the handler. What is the problem?

code.title: checkout-server.ts

o: 2,000 ms is too short for gRPC calls between services.
The two calls should run sequentially (they already do, so nothing is wrong).

The downstream deadlines ignore the caller's budget. After the caller gives up at 300 ms, Checkout keeps working for up to 4 s and may reserve stock for an order nobody will see. Derive deadlines from call.getDeadline() and stop when the call is cancelled.
Deadlines must be set on the server, not on the client.
qs.e: Deadline propagation means each hop gets “whatever time is left”, not a fresh budget. Without it, work continues after the user has already seen an error, which wastes capacity and causes side effects (reserved stock) for failed requests. “Deadlines are set on the server” is the tempting confusion: the client sets the deadline; the server reads it and passes the remainder on.

qs.s: A CreateOrder gRPC call returns DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. Can the client simply retry it?
o: Yes. DEADLINE_EXCEEDED means the server never received the request.

Not blindly. The server may have finished the work after the client stopped waiting. Retry only if the request carries an idempotency key (for example a request_id field) that the server deduplicates on.
No. gRPC does not allow retries.
Yes. HTTP/2 stream IDs let the server detect the duplicate automatically.
qs.e: The deadline is a client-side timer. The server may still be running, or may have committed just after the deadline. gRPC does support retries (retry policy in the service config), but only for idempotent methods or with an application-level key. Stream IDs are per connection and mean nothing for deduplication.

qs.s: Read this .proto. Some messages arrive where status was never set. What is wrong with the design?

code.title: payment.proto

o: proto3 enums cannot be extended later.
Enum numbers must start at 1 in proto3.
Old clients crash when they receive a value they do not know.
In proto3 an unset field reads as its default, the enum value 0. A payment with no status decodes as PAID. The first value should be PAYMENT_STATUS_UNSPECIFIED = 0.
qs.e: proto3 does not send fields that hold their default value, and readers see 0 for anything missing. Making 0 a real business state turns “unknown” into “paid”. The protobuf style guide requires a zero value named ..._UNSPECIFIED. The crash answer is tempting, but proto3 enums are open: an unknown number is kept as an integer, not an error (your switch statement can still mishandle it).

interview.q: Why would you choose gRPC for service-to-service calls, and what operational problems come with it?
answer: Benefits: one contract (.proto) with generated typed clients in every language, compact binary messages, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming, deadlines and cancellation built in.
Load balancing: long-lived connections defeat L4 balancing; you need client-side balancing or an L7 proxy/mesh.
Debugging: binary payloads need grpcurl, reflection and good logging; browsers need gRPC-Web or Connect.
Deadlines are not set by default; you must set and propagate them, and choose status codes and retry policy deliberately.
Contract discipline: buf lint/buf breaking in CI, reserved fields, versioned packages.

interview.q: How do you evolve a .proto contract without breaking running clients?
answer: Add fields with new numbers; never change a field's number or type; never reuse a deleted number or name (mark them reserved).
Readers must handle missing fields (defaults) and unknown enum values.
Enums start with an _UNSPECIFIED = 0 value so “not set” is never a real state.
Renames are safe on the wire (binary uses numbers) but break JSON mapping and generated code; treat them carefully.
Real breaking changes go into a new package version (pricing.v2) served side by side, with buf breaking guarding the old one.
followups: What happens when an old client receives a field it does not know?
Is changing int32 to int64 safe?

interview.q: How does load balancing work for gRPC in Kubernetes, and why is it different from REST?
answer: gRPC keeps one long-lived HTTP/2 connection and multiplexes many requests on it.
A ClusterIP Service balances at connection time (L4), so each client sticks to one pod; scaling up does not spread load.
Options: client-side round_robin over a headless Service (DNS returns all pod IPs), an L7 proxy (Envoy), or a service mesh that balances per request.
Servers set max_connection_age so clients reconnect and discover new pods.
Health checks use grpc.health.v1 so balancers remove unhealthy pods.

one: Rules for changing an API without breaking clients that already depend on it.
an: Renovating a shop while it stays open. You can add new shelves any time; you cannot move the door while customers are walking through it.
how: Additive changes are safe: new optional fields, new endpoints. Breaking changes: removing or renaming fields, changing types, making optional inputs required, changing meaning.
Strategies: version in the URL (/v2/orders), in a header, or date-based versions (Stripe). Or avoid versions by only ever making additive changes.
Clients should be tolerant readers: ignore unknown fields instead of failing.
why: Mobile apps stay installed for years. Once a version ships, you cannot force every user to update, so the server must keep speaking the old contract.
trade: Every live version is code you maintain. Deprecate with dates, measure who still calls old versions, and remove them deliberately.

myth.m: Renaming a field is a small change.
myth.r: To every existing client it is a deletion plus an addition. Add the new field, keep the old one, migrate clients, then remove.

q.s: You need to rename user.name to user.fullName. iOS app versions from last year are still in use. Safest path?
o: Rename it, old apps will update
Return both fields, migrate clients, track usage of the old one, remove it later
Create /v7 for this one field
Rename it in the DB only
q.e: Expand, migrate, contract. The same pattern applies to database columns.

Measuring usage of deprecated fields before removing them

Add logging that records which clients still read a deprecated field.
Run oasdiff (or openapi-diff) between two versions of an OpenAPI spec and see breaking changes detected.

plain:
Once other apps use your API, you cannot freely change it. Some changes are safe (adding a new optional field). Others break existing clients (removing or renaming a field, changing a type).

Versioning and careful migration let you change the API without breaking apps that are already installed on users' phones.
bridge: If you have ever had a frontend crash because the backend renamed userName to username, you have felt a breaking change. Mobile apps make it worse: old versions stay installed for years.

walk.title: Renaming a field safely
steps: Goal: rename name to fullName.
Step 1 (expand): the API returns both name and fullName. Nothing breaks.
Step 2 (migrate): update the web app and release a new mobile version using fullName.
Step 3 (measure): log which clients still read name. Wait until old app versions are almost gone.
Step 4 (contract): remove name. Announce it with a date beforehand.

terms: A change that makes existing clients fail.
Adding something optional; safe for old clients.
Marking something as “will be removed”, with a date.
Add the new thing, migrate, then remove the old thing.
insights: The cheapest versioning strategy is to only ever make additive changes.
Adding a new value to an enum can break clients with exhaustive switches. Treat it as a possible breaking change.

prod.summary: In production, versioning is mostly about knowing who uses what. Seniors make additive changes the default, detect breaking changes automatically in CI, announce removals with standard headers and a date, and remove old versions only after metrics show that traffic has really gone. Mobile apps make this slow: some users never update.
checklist: CI runs a breaking-change diff on the API contract (oasdiff for OpenAPI, buf breaking for Protobuf, a schema registry for GraphQL) and blocks merges that break it.
Usage of every deprecated field and version is measured per client (API key, app version, User-Agent) before anyone schedules removal.
Deprecated endpoints send the Deprecation header (RFC 9745) and the Sunset header (RFC 8594) with the removal date, plus a link to the migration guide.
The mobile app sends its version in a header, and the backend can force an update screen for versions that are too old (a “minimum supported version” check).
Enums in responses are documented as open: clients must handle unknown values. New enum values are announced like breaking changes.
Each live version has an owner and an end date. More than two or three live major versions is a cost problem, not a feature.
numbers: Stripe pins each account to the API version from its first request and uses dated versions (for example 2024-06-20); a request can override it with the Stripe-Version header.
RFC 9745 (March 2025) standardises the Deprecation header; its value is a structured date such as Deprecation: @1688169599 (Unix seconds).
RFC 8594 defines the Sunset header, an HTTP date after which the resource is expected to stop responding.
failures: After a backend deploy, the iOS app crashes on launch for users on older versions only.

A field the old app decodes as required was removed or renamed, or its type changed (number to string). Fix: roll back, restore the field, add a contract diff check to CI, and use expand → migrate → contract.
The Android app shows a blank list after the backend added a new status value "on_hold".

The app parsed the enum strictly and failed on the unknown value. Fix on the client: map unknown values to a fallback. Fix in process: treat new enum values as potentially breaking and check client versions first.
You removed /v1 on the announced date, and a large partner's integration broke.
Removal was based on the calendar, not on traffic. Fix: monitor /v1 calls per API key, contact the remaining callers directly, and use brown-outs (short planned failures) before the final removal.
Three major versions are live and each bug fix must be made three times.
Versions were created for small changes. Fix: version only for true breaking changes, translate old versions to the newest one in a thin adapter layer (the Stripe approach), and set end dates.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Deprecation: @1767225600
Sunset: Wed, 30 Jun 2027 23:59:59 GMT
Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"; type="text/html"

{
  "id": "u_42",
  "name": "Aziza Karimova",
  "fullName": "Aziza Karimova"
}
code.note: The response returns both name (old) and fullName (new) during the expand phase. Deprecation says when it was deprecated (here 1 Jan 2026), and Sunset says when it will stop working.

qs.s: Which change to a JSON response is most likely to break existing clients?
o: Adding a new optional field avatarUrl
Changing price from the number 19.99 to the string "19.99"
Adding a new endpoint GET /v1/reviews
Making the response faster with a cache
qs.e: A type change breaks every typed client (Swift, Kotlin, generated TS) and any code that does math on the value. Adding optional fields or endpoints is additive and safe for tolerant clients. Caching does not change the contract.

qs.s: Logs show 3% of /v1 traffic still comes from app version 2.3, released 2 years ago. The sunset date is next week. What is the best next step?
o: Remove /v1 on the date as announced; 3% is small
Keep /v1 forever
Return random 500s to make those users update
Show a forced-update screen to app versions below the minimum, then remove /v1 after traffic drops
qs.e: 3% of users with a broken app is a lot of support tickets. A forced-update screen (based on the app version header) gives those users a clear path, and then removal is safe. Keeping it forever has a cost; random failures are hostile and look like an outage.

qs.s: A team uses URL versioning (/v1, /v2). A developer wants to add an optional ?include=items parameter. Where should it go?
o: Only in a new /v3
Into both v1 and v2, because it is a breaking change
Into the current version (v2) without a new version, because it is additive
Nowhere; query parameters cannot be versioned
qs.e: An optional parameter does not change behaviour for anyone who does not send it, so it is additive. A new major version for every addition multiplies maintenance. Back-porting to v1 is possible but optional, not required.

qs.s: Read the response diff from a PR. Which statement is correct?

code.title: GET /v1/orders/{id} response diff
code.src:
"id": "o_77",
-  "total": 4200,
+  "total": "42.00",
+  "currency": "USD",
   "status": "paid"

o: Adding currency breaks strict clients; changing total is fine because the value is the same.
Both changes are safe, because JSON is dynamically typed.
Only status is risky, because it is an enum.

Changing total from a number to a string is breaking (typed clients fail to decode it, and JavaScript code doing total / 100 now gets a wrong answer). Adding currency is additive and safe for tolerant readers.
qs.e: A type change is a removal plus an addition. Swift/Kotlin decoders throw, and JS code silently computes nonsense ("42.00" / 100 is 0.42). The safe path is a new field (totalDecimal or amount object) next to the old one. Adding a field only breaks clients that reject unknown fields, which is a client bug the tolerant-reader rule exists to prevent.

qs.s: The server adds a new order status, "refunded". What happens in the shipped mobile app that contains this code?

code.title: badge.ts

o: TypeScript reports a compile error, so the app cannot ship with this bug.
It throws at runtime for refunded orders. TypeScript types do not check data from the server. Add a fallback branch (a neutral badge) and treat new enum values as potentially breaking.
It returns undefined and the badge is simply empty.
JSON.parse fails before the code runs.
qs.e: The Status type is a promise the server can break at any time; the compiler only checked the old union. The exhaustive switch plus throw turns a new value into a crash (often inside a list, which blanks the whole screen). The compile-error answer is tempting, but it only happens when you update the type, which the already-installed app never does.

qs.s: Your API has 300 B2B integrators. You must change the meaning of a field (amounts move from major units to minor units). Which approach keeps most integrators working with the least code to maintain?
o: Date-based versions pinned per account (the Stripe model): the core code implements only the newest behaviour, and a chain of small “version change” transforms converts responses for accounts pinned to older dates.
Copy every endpoint into /v2 and keep both code paths forever.
A feature flag per customer for this one field.
Announce the change and switch everyone in 30 days.
qs.e: Per-account pinning means nobody breaks until they choose to upgrade, and the transform layer keeps old versions as thin adapters instead of parallel codebases. /v2 copies are the tempting “clean” option, but every bug fix must then be made twice, and integrators must migrate everything at once. A 30-day switch breaks many of the 300 who never read the email.

qs.s: It is October 2026. This endpoint still answers normally. What is true?

code.title: Response headers
code.src:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Deprecation: @1767225600
Sunset: Tue, 30 Jun 2026 23:59:59 GMT
Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"

o: HTTP clients automatically stop calling an endpoint after its Sunset date.
The headers are invalid, because the Deprecation date is after the Sunset date.

The Sunset date has passed, but the headers are only hints; nothing stops working until the team turns it off. Before doing that, check who still calls it, contact them, and run short planned brown-outs.
Browsers block requests to an endpoint after its Sunset date.
qs.e: Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) inform clients; no client library acts on them. @1767225600 is 1 January 2026, which is before 30 June 2026, so the headers are consistent. Removal is a decision you make from traffic data, not something the header does for you.

interview.q: How would you version a public API that has mobile clients you cannot force to update?
answer: Default to additive changes only; most “versions” are avoided by adding fields and endpoints instead of changing them.
For real breaking changes, pick one scheme: URL major versions (/v2) for rare big redesigns, or date-based per-account versions with a transform layer for frequent small changes.
Clients must be tolerant readers: ignore unknown fields, map unknown enum values to a fallback.
Apps send their version; the backend can show a forced-update screen below a minimum supported version.
Measure usage per client version before removing anything; announce with Deprecation/Sunset headers and docs.

How do you test that old app versions still work?

interview.q: What counts as a breaking change? Give examples that are not obvious.
answer: Obvious: removing or renaming a field, changing a type, making an optional input required.
Adding an enum value that clients switch on exhaustively.
Making validation stricter (a 50-character name that used to pass now fails), or changing a default value.
Changing a field from never-null to sometimes-null, changing sort order, or changing the default page size.
Changing error codes or status codes that clients branch on, or lowering rate limits.
Changing the meaning while keeping the shape (amounts in cents instead of units) — the most dangerous, because no tool detects it.
followups: Which of these can a diff tool like oasdiff catch?
How would you roll out a stricter validation rule?

interview.q: How do you decide that a deprecated version can actually be removed?
answer: Traffic data per API key, app version and User-Agent, not the calendar.
Contact the remaining large callers directly; email lists are not enough.
Brown-outs: planned short windows where the old version returns errors, so forgotten integrations surface while rollback is easy.
For mobile, wait until the remaining versions are below an agreed threshold and force-update them.
Keep a fast rollback path for the removal itself, and an owner for the decision.

one: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Essential wherever retries happen.
an: Pressing the elevator button five times still brings one elevator. A payment endpoint must behave like that button.
how: HTTP already says which methods are idempotent. GET, PUT and DELETE are: repeating them leaves the same state (a second DELETE may return 404, but nothing more is deleted). POST and PATCH are not, so those are the ones that need protection.
Pattern: the client sends an Idempotency-Key header (a UUID per logical action). The server stores key → result. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.
Message consumers do the same with message IDs, because queues deliver at least once.
why: Retries are everywhere: mobile clients, load balancers, queue consumers, users double-clicking. Idempotency makes retries safe, which makes the whole system more robust.
trade: You need storage for keys with an expiry and a way to handle two identical requests arriving at the same moment (a unique constraint or a lock on the key).

myth.m: Disabling the submit button after click prevents double charges.
myth.r: It stops one double-click. It does nothing about network retries, timeouts or a user refreshing. The server must be idempotent.

q.s: A payment request times out on the client. The server actually completed it. The client retries. What makes this safe?
o: A longer timeout
The client reuses the same Idempotency-Key, and the server returns the stored result
Using PUT instead of POST alone
HTTPS
q.e: The key ties the retry to the original attempt. A longer timeout reduces how often it happens but cannot eliminate it.

more: Where to store keys and for how long
Concurrent duplicates: locking the key while the first request runs
Same key with a different body: reject with 422
Natural idempotency (PUT, upserts, unique constraints) vs keys
Idempotent consumers: deduplicating by message ID
lab: Build POST /payments that "charges" (writes a row). Call it twice with the same body: two rows.
Add an Idempotency-Key header and an idempotency_keys table with a unique constraint. Repeat: one row, same response.

Read how Stripe does it and compare.

plain:
An action is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Reading data is naturally idempotent. Charging a card is not: doing it twice charges twice.

Networks fail in a nasty way: sometimes the server finished the work but the reply got lost. The client cannot know, so it retries. Idempotency makes that retry safe.
bridge: Disabling the “Pay” button after a click stops double-clicks, but not this: the user's phone loses signal, the app retries automatically, and the server charges again. Only the server can fully prevent it.

walk.title: A payment retry that does not double-charge
steps: When the user taps “Pay”, the app generates a random ID: Idempotency-Key: 7f3c....
The server receives it, sees it has never seen this key, charges the card, and saves “key 7f3c → result: success, payment 991”.
The response is lost on the way back. The app times out and retries with the same key.
The server sees key 7f3c is already done and returns the saved result. No second charge.
The app shows “Payment successful”. The user never knew anything went wrong.

terms: Same effect whether done once or many times.
A unique ID the client sends so the server can detect repeats.
A delivery guarantee where messages may arrive more than once.
insights: Anything involving money, emails, SMS or stock must be idempotent.
Add automatic retries only after the server can deduplicate. Retries without idempotency turn every network hiccup into a possible double charge.

prod.summary: In production, idempotency is what makes retries safe: mobile clients on bad networks, load balancers, queue consumers and webhook providers all repeat requests. Seniors make every money-moving or message-sending operation idempotent, store the key and its result atomically with the business change, and handle the hard case: two copies of the same request arriving at the same moment.
checklist: The key is generated by the client once per user action (when the checkout screen opens or the button is first pressed), and reused on every retry of that action. A new key per HTTP attempt makes it useless.
Saving the key and doing the side effect happen in one database transaction, or the key row is written first with status “in progress” and a unique constraint.
A second request with the same key while the first is still running gets 409 Conflict (or waits), not a second execution.
The same key with a different request body is rejected (422 per the IETF draft), so a client bug cannot reuse a key for a different payment.
Keys are scoped to the caller (account or API key) so two customers cannot collide, and they expire after a fixed time (for example 24 hours).
Calls to external providers pass your idempotency key on (Stripe, payment gateways), because your own retry of their call can also double-charge.
Consumers of queues and webhooks deduplicate by message/event ID with a unique constraint, not with a check-then-insert in application code.
numbers: Stripe idempotency keys can be up to 255 characters long, and Stripe may remove them after they are at least 24 hours old.
IETF draft Idempotency-Key header: reuse with a different payload → 422; retry while the original is still processing → 409; missing key on an endpoint that requires it → 400.
RFC 9110: PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST and PATCH are not.
failures: Customers are charged twice, even though the endpoint checks the idempotency table first.

Check-then-insert race: two requests both read “key not found” and both charge. Fix: a unique constraint on (account_id, key) and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING as the first step; only the request that inserted the row proceeds.
Retries still create duplicate orders, although the app sends an Idempotency-Key.
The app generates a new UUID inside the HTTP client for every attempt. Fix: generate the key when the user starts the action and keep it until the action succeeds or is abandoned.
After a crash in the middle of a request, every retry gets 409 forever.

The key was saved as “in progress” and never updated. Fix: record a lock timeout (for example locked_at) and let a retry take over after it expires, or keep the key and the business change in one transaction so a crash rolls back both.
Your system shows one order, but the payment provider shows two charges.
Your retry of the provider call did not send an idempotency key to the provider. Fix: derive a provider key from your own key (for example order_42_charge) and send it on every attempt.

code.title: Idempotent POST /payments: claim the key, call the provider outside the transaction, store the result
code.note: Step 1 is the only place where concurrency is decided: a duplicate in flight blocks on the uncommitted row or finds it locked and gets 409. The provider call is not inside a database transaction, so no row lock or pooled connection is held for seconds while a remote API answers. If the process crashes after step 2, the lock expires after 60 seconds and a retry repeats step 2 with the same provider key, so the customer is charged once.

qs.s: Two identical requests with the same Idempotency-Key arrive 5 ms apart. The handler does SELECT the key → if missing, charge → INSERT the key. What can happen?
o: Both requests see no key and both charge the card
The second request always waits automatically
Postgres rejects the second SELECT
Nothing; 5 ms is enough time for the first insert
qs.e: Check-then-act is a race: both SELECTs run before either INSERT. A SELECT does not lock a row that does not exist yet. The fix is to insert first with a unique constraint, so the database decides which request wins.

qs.s: Which operation is idempotent without any key?
o: POST /orders that creates a new order
PATCH /accounts/1 with { "balanceDelta": -50 }
PUT /users/7/avatar that replaces the avatar with the uploaded image
POST /emails/send
qs.e: Replacing a resource with the same content gives the same final state no matter how many times it runs. Creating, adding a delta, or sending an email changes state on every call. Note that a PATCH can be idempotent (setting a value) or not (adding to it), depending on its body.

qs.s: A mobile app stores the Idempotency-Key in memory for the checkout screen. The app crashes after tapping “Pay”, and the user reopens it and pays again. Was the user charged twice?
o: No, the server recognises the device ID
Possibly yes: the key was lost with the crash, so the second tap uses a new key
No, idempotency keys are tied to the card number
Yes, always, because keys only work for network retries
qs.e: The key only connects attempts that carry it. A new key after a crash looks like a new purchase. To cover this, persist the key with the pending order on the device, or let the server detect duplicates by business data (same cart, same user, within N minutes) and ask the user.

qs.s: The backend implements Idempotency-Key correctly. Read the client. Why do network retries still create duplicate payments?

code.title: pay.ts

o: fetch does not send custom headers on POST.
The backoff is too short; 500 ms is not enough for the server to finish.
A new key is generated for every attempt, so the server sees three different actions. Generate the key once per user action (outside the loop) and reuse it on every retry.
crypto.randomUUID() is not random enough and can collide.
qs.e: The key identifies the logical action, not the HTTP attempt. With a fresh UUID per attempt, the server correctly treats each retry as new. Longer backoff is tempting, but it only changes timing: if the first attempt succeeded and its response was lost, any retry with a new key charges again.

qs.s: This SQL runs inside one transaction for every order.paid message. The queue delivers at least once. What happens when the same message is delivered twice?

code.title: consumer.sql

o: Points are added twice. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING skips the insert silently, but the code never checks whether a row was inserted. It must check the affected row count and skip the UPDATE when it is 0.
The second delivery fails, because ON CONFLICT raises an error and rolls back the transaction.
It works, but processed_messages grows forever, which is the real bug.
It only works under SERIALIZABLE isolation.
qs.e: DO NOTHING means “no error, zero rows affected”. Deduplication only works if the next steps depend on that result (RETURNING or rowCount). The tempting answer assumes a conflict throws; that is what a plain INSERT without ON CONFLICT would do. Table growth is real but is a cleanup task, not the correctness bug.

qs.s: POST /cart/items/7/increment adds one item. On bad networks, retries add extra items. Which redesign removes the need for an idempotency key?
o: PATCH /cart/items/7 with {"op": "increment"}.
Disable the button for one second after each tap.
Return Cache-Control: no-store so proxies do not replay it.
PUT /cart/items/7 with {"quantity": 3}: the client sends the final value, so repeating the request gives the same result.
qs.e: “Set to 3” is naturally idempotent; “add 1” is not. Changing the method to PATCH is the tempting answer, but the body still says “increment”, so it is exactly as unsafe. Absolute values can still lose concurrent updates from two devices, which is where ETag/If-Match comes in.

qs.s: The server keeps idempotency keys for 24 hours. The mobile app queues payments made offline and retries them for up to 3 days with the same key. Is that safe?
o: Yes. The payment provider also deduplicates, so the server's retention does not matter.

No. A retry after 24 hours finds no key, so the payment runs again. The key retention must be longer than the longest client retry window, or the client must stop retrying and check the order status instead.
Yes. UUID keys never collide, so the retry is recognised.
No. The server should return 410 Gone for keys older than 24 hours, and that is enough.
qs.e: Deduplication only works while you still remember the key. The provider answer is tempting, but providers expire keys too (Stripe may remove keys after 24 hours). A 410 for “expired key” requires remembering the key, which is the thing you deleted. Design the retry window and the retention together.

interview.q: Design an idempotent payment endpoint. Walk me through the data model and the concurrency cases.
answer: Client generates one key per user action and reuses it on every retry; the server scopes keys by account.
Table with a unique key on (account_id, key), a hash of the request body, a lock timestamp and the stored response.
Claim the key with a single INSERT … ON CONFLICT; a concurrent duplicate gets 409 (in progress) or waits; a finished key replays the stored response; a different body gets 422.
Do not hold a database transaction open across the provider call; pass a derived idempotency key to the provider, then record the result in a short transaction.
Crash recovery: a stale lock (no response after N seconds) can be taken over, which is safe because the provider call is itself idempotent.
Retention longer than the longest client retry window, and cleanup of old keys.

interview.q: Is exactly-once delivery possible? How do you get exactly-once effects?
answer: Over an unreliable network, a sender cannot know if a lost reply means “not done” or “done”, so delivery is at-most-once or at-least-once.
Systems choose at-least-once and make the receiver idempotent: deduplicate by message ID, or make the operation naturally idempotent (set, upsert).
The dedupe record and the side effect must be committed atomically (same transaction), or the gap reopens.
Side effects outside your database (email, provider calls) need their own keys or accept rare duplicates.
“Exactly-once” features in tools (Kafka transactions) apply inside that tool's boundary, not to your external effects.

interview.q: A client times out calling your API, which calls Stripe. How do you make sure the customer is charged exactly once end to end?
answer: Client: one Idempotency-Key per checkout action, reused on retry.
Your API: dedupe on that key and replay the stored result.
Provider: send a provider idempotency key derived from yours on every attempt, so your own retry cannot double-charge.
Recovery: if your process dies after the provider charged, a retry or a reconciliation job finds the charge (by key or metadata) and records it.
Reconciliation compares your payments with the provider's list daily to catch anything the above missed.

How do you show the user the right status while this is unresolved?

  participant PSP as Payment provider

diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R1 as Request 1
  participant R2 as Request 2 (same key)
  participant DB as Keys table
  R1->>DB: INSERT key 7f3c (unique)
  R2->>DB: INSERT key 7f3c (unique)

  DB-->>R2: conflict, 0 rows claimed

  R2-->>R2: return 409 Conflict, do nothing
diagrams.caption: A “check, then insert” in app code lets both requests pass the check. The unique constraint lets exactly one win; the other gets 409 and the client retries later.

one: Returning large lists in chunks. Offset pagination is simple; cursor pagination is stable and fast at scale.
an: Offset is "skip the first 10,000 pages, then read 20". Cursor is a bookmark: "continue after this exact item".
how: Offset: ?limit=20&offset=10000 → LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000. The DB still walks past 10,000 rows, so deep pages get slow. Inserts during browsing shift items so users see duplicates or miss rows.
Cursor / keyset: ?after=2026-09-01T10:00Z_8812 → WHERE (created_at, id) < (...) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. Uses an index, constant speed at any depth, stable under inserts.
Cursors are usually opaque base64 strings so clients do not depend on their contents.
why: Infinite scroll and feeds are cursor-shaped. Admin tables that jump to page 37 are offset-shaped. Pick per use case.
trade: Cursors cannot jump to an arbitrary page and need a unique, ordered sort key (add the id as a tie-breaker).

myth.r: COUNT(*) on a big filtered table can cost more than the page itself. Many products show "10,000+" for a reason.

q.s: An infinite feed sorted by newest shows duplicate posts while users scroll, during busy hours. Cause and fix?
o: Slow DB; add cache
New posts shift offsets; switch to cursor pagination on (created_at, id)
CORS
Too-high TTL
q.e: Every new post pushes everything down one slot, so the next offset page repeats an item. A cursor continues after a fixed item.

Bidirectional cursors (before/after)
Stable sort with a unique tie-breaker
Estimated counts (Postgres reltuples) vs exact counts
Relay-style connections in GraphQL

Time OFFSET 900000 LIMIT 20 with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
Add an index on (created_at, id) and time the keyset version of the same page.
Build the endpoint returning {items, nextCursor}.
