plain:
You never return a million rows at once. You return pages. There are two common ways.

Offset: “skip 40, give me 20”. Simple, lets you jump to page 37, but gets slow for deep pages and shows duplicates when new rows are inserted. Cursor: “give me 20 after this item”. Fast at any depth and stable, but you cannot jump to a page number.
bridge: Infinite scroll with React Query's useInfiniteQuery and a nextCursor is cursor pagination. A table with page numbers at the bottom is usually offset pagination.

walk.title: Why the feed shows the same post twice
steps: The feed uses offset: page 1 is OFFSET 0 LIMIT 20, page 2 is OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20.
The user reads page 1. Meanwhile, 3 new posts are published at the top.
Everything shifts down by 3. Page 2 now starts with the last 3 posts the user already saw.
Switch to cursor: page 1 returns 20 posts plus nextCursor = the time and ID of the last post.
Page 2 asks for posts older than that exact post. New posts at the top do not matter. No duplicates.

terms: Continue after a specific item, using a sorted unique key.
A cursor encoded so clients treat it as a token, not data to parse.
A second sort field (like ID) so the order is always unique.
insights: Use cursor pagination for feeds and public APIs; use offset for admin tables where users jump to page numbers.
Switching a public endpoint from offset to cursor later is a breaking change, so choose cursor for public lists from day one.

prod.summary: In production, pagination is a performance and correctness feature. Seniors check that every list has a server-side maximum page size, that deep pages do not turn into full-table scans, that the sort order is fully unique so no row is skipped or repeated, and that “total count” is not quietly costing more than the page itself.
checklist: The server enforces a maximum page size (for example 100) no matter what the client sends.
The sort order ends with a unique column (ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC). Without a tie-breaker, rows with equal timestamps can appear on two pages or on none.
There is a composite index that matches the filter + sort exactly, for example (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC), and EXPLAIN shows an index scan with no separate Sort step.
Cursors are opaque (base64url of the last key) and validated on input; a tampered cursor returns 400, not a 500.
The cursor encodes the sort key, not only an ID, and changing the sort or filters invalidates the cursor.
Exact totals are either removed, cached, capped (“10,000+”), or replaced by an estimate. COUNT(*) over millions of rows on every request is a common hidden cost.
The response tells the client whether there is a next page (nextCursor: null at the end), usually by fetching limit + 1 rows.
numbers: GitHub REST API: per_page max 100, and the next page URL is in the Link header.
GitHub GraphQL API: first/last must be between 1 and 100 on every connection.
PostgreSQL docs: rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server, so a large OFFSET can be slow.
failures: Page 1 loads in 20 ms, page 2,000 takes 3 seconds, and DB CPU spikes when a crawler walks the list.
OFFSET 40000 reads and throws away 40,000 rows each time. Fix: keyset pagination with a matching index; cap the maximum offset for any remaining offset UI.
Users report items missing from an export that pages through the API.

The sort was ORDER BY created_at only. Many rows share the same timestamp (bulk import), so page boundaries cut through them non-deterministically. Fix: add id as a tie-breaker in both ORDER BY and the cursor.
The list endpoint is slow even for page 1. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows most time in Aggregate over a Seq Scan.
The response includes total, computed with COUNT(*) over a big filtered table on every request. Fix: drop or cache the count, show “1,000+”, or use an estimate from EXPLAIN / pg_class.reltuples.
Keyset query is still slow; the plan shows Index Scan followed by a Sort node.

The index column order or direction does not match the ORDER BY, or the filter column is missing from the index. Fix: create an index in the same order, for example (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC).

code.title: Keyset pagination with an opaque, validated, full-precision cursor
code.note: Two details matter. The row comparison (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) with the matching index lets Postgres jump straight to the next row. And the cursor time comes from created_at::text: Postgres stores microseconds, but node-postgres returns a JS Date with only milliseconds, and a rounded cursor silently skips rows. String(last.id) matters for serial/int ids: node-postgres returns them as JS numbers, and without it every second page fails the cursor check with 400.

qs.s: An endpoint uses ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 20 with a cursor that stores only the last score. Many items have the same score. What will users see?
o: Correct results, because scores are sorted
An error from Postgres
Faster pages, because fewer columns are compared
Skipped or repeated items at page boundaries
qs.e: With WHERE score < last_score, all other items with the same score as the last one are skipped. With <= they repeat. A unique tie-breaker (score, id) in both the ORDER BY and the cursor fixes it.

qs.s: An admin table needs “jump to page 37” and has 5,000 rows. A teammate wants to rewrite it with cursors. Your view?
o: Keep offset: 5,000 rows is small, and users need page numbers
Cursors are always better; rewrite it
Use offset but drop the index
Load all 5,000 rows into the browser and paginate there, always
qs.e: Offset's cost grows with the offset; at 5,000 rows it is trivial, and page jumping is a real requirement cursors cannot meet. Cursors matter for large tables, infinite feeds and public APIs. Loading everything client-side can be fine for tiny lists but does not scale as a rule.

qs.s: Your API returns { items, total }. The posts table has 40 million rows. total uses COUNT(*) with the same filters. Page queries take 5 ms; the full request takes 900 ms. What is the best fix?
o: Add more DB connections
Remove or approximate total (for example “10,000+” or a cached estimate)
Switch to offset pagination
Increase the page size to 1,000
qs.e: The page uses an index and stops after 20 rows, but an exact COUNT must visit every matching row. Most UIs only need “there is more”. More connections and bigger pages do not reduce the counting work.

qs.s: Users see some posts twice when they scroll. Read the keyset query. What is the bug?

code.title: next-page.sql
code.src:
-- $1 = created_at of the last row, $2 = its id
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM posts
WHERE created_at < $1 OR id < $2
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

o: LIMIT 20 should be LIMIT 21.

OR id < $2 also matches newer posts that happen to have a smaller id, so already-seen rows come back. The condition must be (created_at, id) < ($1, $2), which means created_at < $1 OR (created_at = $1 AND id < $2).
The sort should be ascending for keyset pagination to work.
Keyset pagination cannot use two columns; use only created_at.
qs.e: The tie-breaker (id) only matters when created_at is equal. With a plain OR, any row with a smaller id passes, even if it is newer than the cursor. The row-value comparison is both correct and index-friendly. Using only created_at is the tempting simplification, but rows with equal timestamps would then be skipped or repeated at page boundaries.

qs.s: Read this EXPLAIN ANALYZE for page 1 of a tenant's feed (2.4 s). Which change fixes it?

code.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
code.src:
Limit  (actual time=2412.551..2412.560 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=2412.549..2412.553 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: created_at DESC, id DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 27kB
        ->  Seq Scan on posts  (actual time=0.012..1650.330 rows=3800000 loops=1)
              Filter: (tenant_id = 17)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 21000000

o: Raise work_mem so the sort fits in memory.
Switch to OFFSET pagination, which does not need a sort.
Add an index on created_at only.
CREATE INDEX ON posts (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC), so Postgres reads the first 20 rows of tenant 17 already in order and stops.
qs.e: The plan reads 24.8 million rows and sorts 3.8 million to return 20. An index that matches the filter and then the sort lets the Limit stop after 20 index entries. work_mem is the tempting answer, but the sort already ran in 27 kB of memory; the cost is the scan, not the sort. An index on created_at alone would walk all tenants' rows in time order and filter most of them out.

qs.s: A user is on page 3 of a keyset-paginated list. Before they load page 4, the row their cursor points to is deleted. What happens on the next request?
o: The API returns 404, because the cursor row no longer exists.
The list restarts from page 1.
It works normally. The query compares values (created_at, id) with the cursor; the row itself does not need to exist.
One page of results is skipped.
qs.e: A keyset cursor is a position in the sort order, not a reference to a row. WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor values) works whether or not that row still exists. This is one advantage over designs that store “after id 991” and then look that row up to find its timestamp; those do break with 404 when the row is gone.

qs.s: An export job pages through events with this code and some events are missing from the export. created_at is timestamptz DEFAULT now(), and many rows are written per millisecond. Why?

code.title: events-page.ts

o: Postgres stores microseconds, but a JS Date keeps only milliseconds. The cursor is rounded down, so rows between the rounded time and the real time of the last row are skipped. Build the cursor from created_at::text (or a microsecond integer) selected in SQL.
base64url encoding loses characters from the ISO string.
Row-value comparisons cannot use an index, so Postgres skips rows.
LIMIT 51 hides the last row of every page.
qs.e: Example: the last row has 10:00:00.123456; the cursor says .123. The next page asks for rows before .123, so a row at .123200 (which comes after the last row in DESC order) is never returned. LIMIT 51 is the tempting answer, but the 51st row is only used to detect a next page and is returned again on the next request.

interview.q: Offset vs cursor pagination: how do you choose, and what does each cost?
answer: Offset: simple, allows “jump to page 37” and totals; cost grows with the offset because skipped rows are still read; inserts and deletes shift pages (duplicates and gaps).
Cursor/keyset: constant cost at any depth with a matching index, stable under inserts; no random page access; needs a unique sort key.
Feeds, infinite scroll, sync and exports → cursor. Small admin tables with page numbers → offset is fine, with a cap on the maximum offset.
Cursors are opaque, encode every sort key, and are tied to the sort and filters they were created with.
Both need a server-side maximum page size.
followups: How do you support “previous page” with cursors?
How would you paginate a search result sorted by relevance?

interview.q: Design pagination for a feed sorted by a score that changes over time (for example “hot” posts).
answer: Keyset on (score, id) breaks when scores change between requests: items move across the cursor and are repeated or skipped.
Option 1: snapshot the ranked list of IDs when the session starts (cache it with a TTL) and paginate over that list.
Option 2: paginate by a stable key (time) and rank within a window, accepting less “perfect” ordering.
Option 3: accept duplicates and remove them on the client by ID; acceptable for some social feeds.
Always add a unique tie-breaker, and decide explicitly what “consistency” the product needs.
followups: How large can the snapshot be before it is a problem?
How do you handle a deleted item inside a snapshot?

interview.q: Product wants an exact total count on a 50-million-row table, filtered per user. What do you do?
answer: Measure first: COUNT(*) with filters may scan millions of rows on every request and cost more than the page itself.
Ask what the number is for. Often “has more” or “1,000+” is enough.
If exact counts are needed: a maintained counter (updated by triggers or in the same transaction), or a cached count refreshed periodically.
For rough numbers: estimates from the planner (EXPLAIN rows) or pg_class.reltuples for whole tables.
Never compute the count on every page request; compute it once per search or not at all.

Why does Postgres need to scan to count rows?

one: Capping how many requests a client can make in a time window, to protect the service and share it fairly.
an: A tap with a flow regulator: you can drink, you just cannot drain the tank.
how: Fixed window: 100 requests per minute, counter resets on the minute. Simple, allows bursts at the boundary.
Sliding window smooths that edge. Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends one; allows short bursts up to bucket size. The most common choice.
Keyed by API key, user ID or IP. With several servers the counters live in a shared store like Redis. Clients get 429 Too Many Requests and a Retry-After header.
why: Protects against abuse, scrapers, buggy clients in retry loops, and runaway costs (especially when each request calls a paid LLM).
trade: Per-IP limits punish users behind a shared NAT (a whole university). Limits on login/OTP endpoints are a security control, not just capacity.

myth.m: Rate limiting is a performance feature I can add later.
myth.r: On OTP, login and anything that costs you money per call, it is a day-one security control. SMS endpoints without limits get abused to send thousands of paid messages.

q.s: Your SMS OTP endpoint has no limits. What is the most likely real-world abuse?
o: Slow page loads
Bots triggering thousands of paid SMS (toll fraud) and brute-forcing codes
CORS errors
Cache misses
q.e: SMS pumping is a known attack that runs up huge bills. Limit per phone number, per IP, and globally; also cap attempts per code.

Atomic counters in Redis (INCR + EXPIRE, Lua scripts)
Rate-limit response headers: Retry-After (RFC 9110) and the IETF draft RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy fields (older drafts used RateLimit-Limit/-Remaining/-Reset)

Abuse-specific limits: per phone number, per account, per OTP code

plain:
Rate limiting means “each client may make at most N requests per time period”. Above that, the server answers 429 Too Many Requests instead of doing the work.

It protects your server from overload, stops abuse (bots, password guessing, spam), and caps costs when each request costs you money (SMS, AI calls).
bridge: You have probably hit GitHub's or OpenAI's rate limits and seen 429. On your own APIs, you are the one setting those limits.

walk.title: Protecting an OTP (SMS code) endpoint
steps: Without limits, a bot calls POST /auth/send-code 50,000 times with random phone numbers. You pay for 50,000 SMS.
Add a limit per phone number: max 3 codes per 10 minutes.
Add a limit per IP: max 20 requests per hour, and a global daily cap on SMS sent.

Store counters in Redis with an expiry, and set the counter and the expiry atomically (one Lua script, or SET key 0 EX 600 NX before INCR). Two separate calls can leave a key with no expiry if the app crashes between them.

Also limit verify attempts: after 5 wrong guesses the code is invalid. A guesser then gets 5 tries out of 1,000,000 possible 6-digit codes per code sent, and only 3 codes per 10 minutes: brute force becomes impractical.

terms: The status code for “too many requests”.
Tokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends one. Allows small bursts.
Count requests per minute (or hour), reset at the boundary.
A header telling the client how long to wait.
insights: Per-IP limits can block whole offices or universities behind one IP. Combine them with per-account limits.
Set limits from real traffic: look at what your heaviest normal clients send per minute, set the limit a few times above that, then tune with the 429 metrics.

prod.summary: In production, rate limiting is layered: a coarse per-IP limit at the edge (CDN, WAF, gateway) against floods, and finer limits in the app per account, per API key and per expensive action (OTP, login, LLM calls). Seniors care that the counters are atomic and shared across instances, that the key identifies the real client (not the load balancer), and that the limiter fails in a deliberate way when Redis is down.
checklist: The limit key uses the real client IP from a trusted proxy header. If the app trusts any X-Forwarded-For, attackers rotate fake IPs; if it trusts none, every user shares the load balancer's IP.

The counter and its expiry are set atomically — a Lua script or MULTI/EXEC (a pipeline alone only saves round trips, it is not atomic). Otherwise a crash between INCR and EXPIRE leaves a key that never expires and blocks that user forever.
Expensive or abusable actions have their own limits: per phone number and per IP for OTP send, per account for login attempts, per user and globally for LLM tokens or spend.
429 responses include Retry-After, and your own clients back off with jitter instead of retrying immediately.
The failure mode is decided: if Redis is unreachable, does the limiter allow (fail open) or block (fail closed)? Usually open for normal APIs, closed for OTP and payments.
Limits are visible in metrics: 429 rate per route and per client. A sudden rise means either an attack or a limit that is too low for a real customer.
Internal service-to-service traffic and health checks are excluded or have separate limits, so one batch job cannot lock out real users.
numbers: GitHub REST API: 5,000 requests per hour for an authenticated user (15,000 for GitHub Apps owned by Enterprise Cloud orgs).
Stripe: 100 requests per second globally per account in live mode, 25 in sandbox, and 25 per second for most individual endpoints.
A fixed window of 100 per minute can let through up to 200 requests in a few seconds: 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next.
failures: Your SMS bill jumps from $50 to $8,000 in one night; logs show OTP requests to thousands of numbers in one country prefix.

SMS pumping (toll fraud): bots trigger messages to premium numbers. Fix: per-number, per-IP and global daily caps on OTP send, a country allowlist, CAPTCHA after the first attempts, and a spend alert.
Every user in the app gets 429 at the same time during normal traffic.
The limiter keys on req.ip, which is the load balancer's IP, so all users share one bucket. Fix: configure trusted proxies (for example Express trust proxy) so the real client IP is used.
Attackers bypass the per-IP login limit by sending a different X-Forwarded-For on every request.
The app trusts the first value in the header, which the client controls. Fix: trust only the IP added by your own proxy (the right-most trusted hop), and add per-account limits.
Limits are not enforced: a client makes 300 requests per minute against a limit of 100.
Each of 3 instances keeps counters in memory. Fix: shared counters in Redis, or a gateway that enforces the limit in one place.

code.title: Atomic fixed-window limiter in Redis (ioredis + Lua)
code.note: If the app ran INCR and then EXPIRE as two separate calls, a crash between them would leave a key with no expiry, and that client would be blocked forever.

qs.s: Your limiter allows 100 requests per minute with a fixed window. A client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:01. How many are allowed?
o: 0, because the client is blocked for burst behaviour
qs.e: Each burst falls into a different window, so both pass: 200 requests in about 2 seconds. Sliding windows or a token bucket smooth this boundary effect.

qs.s: Redis, which stores your rate-limit counters, goes down. Which behaviour is most reasonable?
o: Block all requests everywhere until Redis is back
Fail open for normal API reads, but fail closed for OTP sending and other paid or security-critical actions
Crash the app so Kubernetes restarts it
Switch to per-process in-memory counters and set the limits to zero
qs.e: Blocking all traffic turns a Redis outage into a full outage. Allowing everything on OTP endpoints invites SMS fraud and brute force exactly when protection is gone. Choosing per endpoint is the senior answer. Restarting does not bring Redis back.

qs.s: A university with 20,000 students sits behind one public IP. Students get 429 during exam registration. The limit is 100 requests/minute per IP. Best change?
o: Key limits by authenticated user (and API key), and keep a much higher per-IP limit only as a flood guard
Remove rate limiting during exam periods
Lower the limit to 50 to protect the server better
Block the university IP
qs.e: Per-IP limits punish everyone behind a shared NAT. For logged-in traffic the account is the right identity; a generous per-IP limit still stops floods. Removing limits or blocking the IP trade one problem for a worse one.

qs.s: The app runs behind one AWS load balancer. Attackers try thousands of passwords on /login and are never limited. Read the setup. Why?

code.title: server.ts

o: 10 attempts per 15 minutes is too strict, so the limiter turns itself off.
The limiter keeps counters in memory, which never works.
trust proxy must be true behind a load balancer, so the setup is correct and the problem is elsewhere.

With trust proxy set to true, req.ip is the left-most X-Forwarded-For value, which the client controls. Each request sends a fake IP and gets a fresh bucket. Set it to the number of proxies (1) and add a per-account limit.
qs.e: true trusts every hop, so the attacker's own header wins. With 1, Express takes the address that your load balancer appended, which the client cannot fake. In-memory counters are tempting to blame, but with a single instance they work; they only fail when there are several instances.

qs.s: Calculate: a token bucket has capacity 20 and refills 5 tokens per second. The client was idle for a full minute, then sends 50 requests at the same instant. How many succeed immediately?
qs.e: The bucket never holds more than its capacity, no matter how long the client was idle, so at most 20 requests pass. The other 30 get 429 (then 5 more per second as tokens refill). 50 is the tempting answer if you think idle time “saves up” without limit; capacity is exactly the setting that prevents that.

qs.s: Read the access log after you started returning 429 to the /v1/sync endpoint. What is happening, and what is the fix?

code.src:

12:00:00.012 POST /v1/sync 429 retry-after=30 device=a91f
12:00:00.015 POST /v1/sync 429 retry-after=30 device=a91f
12:00:00.019 POST /v1/sync 429 retry-after=30 device=c03b
...

o: The limit is too low. Raise it until clients stop receiving 429.
Return 503 instead of 429 so clients understand that they should slow down.

A retry storm: the app retries immediately and ignores Retry-After. Fix the client (honour Retry-After, exponential backoff with jitter, a retry cap) and reject these requests cheaply at the edge until the fixed version is out.
The limiter is broken because Retry-After should be shorter.
qs.e: Each device sends several requests per second while being told to wait 30 s. The 429s themselves now cause most of the load. Raising the limit is tempting, but the buggy client would just retry faster against a bigger limit. 503 has the same problem: a client that ignores headers ignores both.

qs.s: Your /chat endpoint calls a paid LLM. The limit is 60 requests per minute per user. One user sends 60 requests per minute, each with a 100,000-token prompt, and your daily bill explodes. What is the right fix?
o: Lower the limit to 10 requests per minute.
Limit by cost: tokens (or money) per user per day, plus a global daily spend cap and a maximum prompt size.
Switch to a per-IP limit.
Cache LLM responses.
qs.e: When requests have very different costs, counting requests does not limit cost. A token or spend budget does, and the global cap protects you from many users at once. Lowering the request limit is tempting, but it hurts normal users and still lets one huge prompt per request through. Caching rarely helps with unique prompts.

interview.q: Design a rate limiter for an API that runs on 20 instances in two regions.
answer: Choose the key: API key or user ID first, IP only as a coarse layer (shared NAT, spoofed headers).
Shared state: Redis per region with atomic updates (a Lua script); accept that limits are per region, or split the global budget between regions.
Algorithm: token bucket or sliding window counter; a fixed window is fine for coarse limits but allows 2× bursts at window edges.
Failure mode: fail open for normal traffic when Redis is down, fail closed for OTP and payments; a local in-memory fallback limiter as backup.
Responses: 429 with Retry-After; metrics on 429 rate per route and per key; limits configurable per plan without a deploy.
Coarse limits at the edge (CDN/WAF) so floods never reach the app.
followups: How do you avoid an extra Redis round trip on every request?
How would you implement per-plan limits?

interview.q: Compare fixed window, sliding window and token bucket. Which would you choose for a public API?
answer: Fixed window: one counter per window; cheapest; up to 2× the limit around the boundary.
Sliding window log: exact, but stores every timestamp; expensive at high volume.
Sliding window counter: weighted mix of current and previous window; close to exact with two counters.
Token bucket: steady refill with a burst size; matches real client behaviour (a page load bursts, then idles). Usual choice for public APIs.
The choice matters less than the key, the atomicity and the failure behaviour.
followups: How would you implement a token bucket in Redis?
What is the difference between a token bucket and a leaky bucket?

interview.q: How would you protect an SMS OTP endpoint from abuse?
answer: Limits on several keys at once: per phone number, per IP or device, per account, and a global daily cap.
Limits on verification: a few attempts per code, then the code is invalid; codes expire after minutes.
Country allowlist and premium-number blocking against SMS pumping (toll fraud).
CAPTCHA or proof-of-work after the first attempts; spend alerts on the SMS provider.
Fail closed: if the limiter store is down, do not send SMS.
followups: What is SMS pumping and how do you detect it?
How do you avoid locking out real users on a shared mobile carrier IP?

one: Instead of you polling another service, it calls a URL on your server when something happens.
an: Leaving your number with the shop so they call you when the item arrives, rather than you phoning every hour.
how: You register an endpoint (e.g. /webhooks/payments). The provider POSTs an event (payment.succeeded) with a JSON body.
Verify the signature: providers sign the body with a shared secret (HMAC). Without verification, anyone can POST fake "payment succeeded" events.

Most providers retry when you return a non-2xx status or respond too slowly (Stripe retries for up to 3 days). Some, like GitHub, do not retry automatically, so you must redeliver missed events yourself. Either way, the same event can arrive more than once and out of order.
why: Payments, GitHub, Stripe, Telegram bots all deliver events this way. It is how your system learns about things that happen outside it.
trade: Respond 2xx fast and do the heavy work in a background job, or the provider times out and retries. Store event IDs to dedupe (idempotency). Reconcile periodically in case some events never arrive.

myth.m: If the provider called my webhook, the event is real and new.
myth.r: Only if the signature checks out, and only if you have not already processed that event ID.

q.s: Your payment webhook handler marks orders paid, then sends an email and generates a PDF. The provider keeps retrying, and customers get 3 emails. Fix?
o: Ask the provider to stop retrying
Verify signature, dedupe by event ID, return 200 quickly, do email/PDF in a background job
Make the handler slower
Disable signatures
q.e: Slow handlers cause timeouts, timeouts cause retries, retries without dedupe cause duplicate side effects.

more: Replay protection with timestamps in the signature
Out-of-order events and using the fetched current state instead of the event body
Retry schedules and endpoint disabling by providers
Sending webhooks yourself: queues, retries, signing, delivery logs
Local development with tunnels (Stripe CLI, ngrok, cloudflared)
lab: Create a Stripe test account and forward events locally with stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhooks.
Verify the signature using the raw body, store the event ID with a unique constraint, return 200 fast, and enqueue the work.
Use stripe events resend to deliver the same event twice and confirm it is processed once.

plain:
A webhook is the reverse of calling an API. Instead of you asking another service “did anything happen?”, it calls a URL on your server when something happens, like “payment succeeded”.

Because it comes from outside, you must check it is real (a signature), and you must handle the same event arriving more than once.
bridge: A Telegram bot receiving messages, Stripe telling you a payment succeeded, and GitHub triggering your Netlify build on push are all webhooks.

walk.title: Handling a payment webhook correctly
steps: The payment provider sends POST /webhooks/payments with { type: 'payment.succeeded', id: 'evt_9', orderId: 42 } and a signature header.
Your server recomputes the signature from the raw body and your shared secret. If it does not match, reject with 400.
Check whether evt_9 was already processed (stored IDs). If yes, return 200 and stop.
Save the event ID, mark order 42 as paid, put “send receipt email” into a background job, and return 200 within a second.
If you were slow or returned 500, the provider would retry later; the duplicate check makes that safe.

terms: An HTTP call from another service to your server when an event happens.
A code proving the request came from the real sender and was not changed.
A unique ID per event, used to ignore duplicates.
A tool that forwards webhooks to your laptop during development.
insights: Treat a webhook as a hint that something changed. The provider's API is the source of truth: when in doubt, fetch the current object.
Test locally with the provider's CLI or a tunnel (stripe listen, ngrok), and include a replayed duplicate event in the test.

prod.summary: In production, a webhook endpoint is a public URL that accepts money-related events from the internet. Seniors verify the signature on the raw body, reject old timestamps, store the event ID with a unique constraint, return 2xx within a second or two, and do the real work in a background job. They also reconcile: a nightly job asks the provider's API what really happened, because some events never arrive.
checklist: The signature is verified against the raw request body. If a JSON body parser runs first and the body is re-serialised, the signature will never match.
The signature check uses a constant-time compare (provider SDKs do this) and rejects events with timestamps outside the tolerance window, which blocks replay attacks.
The event ID is inserted into a table with a unique constraint before any side effect; duplicates return 200 and stop.
The handler only verifies, stores and enqueues, then returns 2xx. Emails, PDFs and calls to other services run in a worker.
Handlers do not trust event order. They either check the object's current state (for example, ignore payment.pending after payment.succeeded) or fetch the latest object from the provider's API.
A reconciliation job compares your records with the provider's API (for example, payments in the last 24 hours) to catch missed events.
Webhook secrets are per environment and can be rotated; the endpoint is monitored for non-2xx responses, because providers disable endpoints that keep failing.
numbers: Stripe retries undelivered events for up to 3 days with exponential backoff in live mode.
Stripe's libraries reject signatures whose timestamp is more than 5 minutes old by default; a tolerance of 0 disables the check.
GitHub expects a 2xx response within 10 seconds, and does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries.
failures: Every webhook fails with “No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload”.

The framework parsed the JSON and the code passed the re-serialised object, not the original bytes. Fix: read the raw body (await req.text() in a Next.js route handler, express.raw() in Express) and verify that.
Customers receive the same receipt email three times.
The handler sends the email inline, takes longer than the provider's timeout, and the provider retries. No event-ID dedupe. Fix: dedupe on event ID, enqueue the email, return 200 fast.
Some orders stay “pending” forever although the customer paid.

The webhook was missed (endpoint down during a deploy, or the provider gave up). Fix: a reconciliation job that lists recent payments from the provider API and fixes mismatches; alert on webhook 5xx rates.
An order goes from “paid” back to “pending”.
Events arrived out of order: payment.pending was processed after payment.succeeded. Fix: only allow forward state transitions, or fetch the current object from the provider before updating.

code.title: Next.js route handler: verify, dedupe, enqueue, return 200
code.note: If enqueueing fails after the insert, the event is marked as seen but never processed. Production code puts the insert and the job in one transaction (an outbox table or a Postgres-backed queue), or the reconciliation job covers the gap.

qs.s: An attacker captures a real, correctly signed payment.succeeded request and sends it again a week later. Which check stops it?
o: The timestamp inside the signed payload is outside the tolerance window, so verification fails
HTTPS prevents replay
The HMAC secret changes every request
The JSON body parser rejects old events
qs.e: Providers like Stripe sign the timestamp together with the body, and the SDK rejects old timestamps (5 minutes by default). Dedupe by event ID also helps. HTTPS protects the connection, but cannot stop someone from re-sending bytes they already have.

qs.s: Your webhook handler runs express.json() and then verifies JSON.stringify(req.body). Signature checks fail for all events. Why?
o: The webhook secret is wrong in every environment
Express does not support POST bodies
The signature must be computed over the exact raw bytes; re-serialising changes spacing and key order
HMAC only works with form-encoded bodies
qs.e: HMAC is computed over exact bytes. JSON.stringify of a parsed object rarely reproduces the original byte-for-byte (whitespace, escaping, number format). Use the raw body for verification. A wrong secret is possible, but would not explain a pattern caused by the code path.

qs.s: GitHub webhooks to your CI service fail for 2 hours during an outage on your side. After you recover, what happens to those events?
o: GitHub retries them automatically for 3 days
GitHub queues them and delivers them when your endpoint returns 200 once
They are lost forever and cannot be recovered
They are not retried automatically; you must redeliver them (manually or via the API)
qs.e: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed webhook deliveries. You can redeliver from the UI or with the REST API by listing failed deliveries. Stripe's 3-day retry is provider-specific; never assume all providers behave the same.

qs.s: This handler has several problems. Which one is most likely to cause duplicate emails in production?

code.title: webhook.ts

o: handle runs before the response and takes about 8 s. The provider times out and retries, and there is no deduplication by event ID, so each retry sends the emails again.
!== is not a constant-time comparison.
express.raw breaks the HMAC, because the body must be parsed JSON.
There is no timestamp check, so attackers can replay events.
qs.e: Slow handler + retries + no dedupe = duplicate side effects. Return 2xx after verifying and storing the event ID, and do the work in a job. The !== issue is real and tempting, but it is a security weakness (timing attack), not a source of duplicates; use crypto.timingSafeEqual. express.raw is actually correct: the HMAC must be computed over the raw bytes.

qs.s: You send webhooks to your customers. One customer's endpoint has been down for 2 days. What should your sending system do?
o: Retry every second until it succeeds, so the customer gets events as soon as possible.
Drop the event after the first failure; customers can poll the API.

Retry from a durable queue with exponential backoff for a limited period, isolated per endpoint so it does not delay other customers; then disable the endpoint, notify the customer, and keep delivery logs with manual redelivery.
Keep one global ordered queue so every customer receives events in exact order.
qs.e: This is what providers like Stripe do: bounded retries with backoff, then disable and notify. Per-endpoint isolation is the part people forget: one global queue is the tempting “ordered” design, but one dead endpoint then blocks every other customer behind it (head-of-line blocking). Retrying every second wastes resources and looks like an attack.

qs.s: Your library follows the Standard Webhooks spec with a 5-minute tolerance. This request has a valid signature. Your server clock reads 1759480900. What happens?

code.title: Incoming request
code.src:
POST /hooks HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
webhook-id: msg_2Ka9
webhook-timestamp: 1759480000
webhook-signature: v1,K5oZfzN95Z9UVu1EsfQmfVNQhnkZ2pj9o9NDDrWiE48=

{"type":"invoice.paid","data":{"id":"inv_31"}}

o: It is accepted, because the signature is valid.
It is rejected as too old: 900 seconds (15 minutes) is outside the 5-minute tolerance. If your clock is wrong rather than the request being a replay, fix NTP on the server.
It is accepted, because only timestamps in the future are rejected.
It is rejected, because v1 signatures are deprecated.
qs.e: The timestamp is part of the signed content (id.timestamp.body), so an attacker cannot change it, and the tolerance check limits how long a captured request can be replayed. Libraries reject timestamps that are too far in the past or the future. “Valid signature means accept” is the tempting answer; the signature proves who sent it, not when.

qs.s: Two subscription.updated events arrive in reverse order: first the one created at 10:00:05 (status active), then the one created at 10:00:01 (status past_due). How should the handler deal with this?
o: Process events in arrival order; the provider guarantees order.
Return 409 for the older event so the provider retries it later in the correct order.
Push both into a FIFO queue so the worker processes them in order.

Do not trust order: compare the event's creation time or object version with what you stored and ignore older updates, or fetch the current subscription from the provider's API before applying a change.
qs.e: Webhook providers generally do not guarantee order. A FIFO queue is the tempting answer, but it keeps arrival order, which is already wrong. Returning 409 just causes retries and does not create order either. Version checks or “fetch the current state” make the handler correct no matter the order.

interview.q: Walk me through building a reliable receiver for payment webhooks.
answer: Verify the signature over the raw body with the provider's SDK (constant-time compare, timestamp tolerance against replay).
Insert the event ID into a table with a unique constraint; duplicates return 200 and stop.
Enqueue the work in the same transaction (outbox or a Postgres-backed queue), return 2xx fast.
Workers apply changes idempotently and handle out-of-order events (forward-only state transitions or fetch current state).
Reconciliation job compares your records with the provider's API to catch missed events; alerts on non-2xx rates.
Per-environment secrets with rotation (accept two secrets during the switch).
followups: How do you rotate the webhook secret without downtime?
What happens if your database is down when the webhook arrives?

interview.q: You are building outgoing webhooks for your own product. What do you need?
answer: Events written to an outbox in the same transaction as the change, then delivered by workers.
Signing (HMAC with a per-endpoint secret, timestamp and message ID in the signed content); the Standard Webhooks spec is a good default.
Retries with exponential backoff and a time limit, per-endpoint isolation, automatic disabling of dead endpoints with notification.
Delivery logs and manual redelivery in a dashboard; a test-event button.
SSRF protection: block internal IP ranges for customer-provided URLs, short timeouts, response size limits.
followups: Why is SSRF a risk here?
Thin events (IDs only) or full payloads: which do you send?

interview.q: A customer says they paid, but their order is still “pending”. How do you investigate?
answer: Find the payment at the provider (dashboard or API) and its event IDs; check the provider's delivery log for your endpoint (status codes, timing).
Search your logs and webhook_events table for those event IDs: never received, rejected (signature), or received but not processed.
If received: check the job queue (failed, stuck, dead-lettered) and the handler's state logic (out-of-order event ignored?).
Fix the order with the reconciliation path, not a manual SQL update, so the same code runs.
Then fix the cause and add the missing alert (signature failure rate, job failures, reconciliation mismatches).
followups: How would you stop this class of bug from reaching customers again?
What would you put in the reconciliation job?

one: How a server handles many requests at once. Node uses one thread with an event loop; Java/Go/.NET use many threads or goroutines.
an: Node is one very fast waiter who never stands at a table waiting; they take an order, move on, and come back when the kitchen rings. A thread-per-request server hires a waiter per table.
how: Most backend time is spent waiting on I/O (DB, network). Node's event loop starts an I/O operation, registers a callback, and serves other requests meanwhile. That is why one Node process handles thousands of concurrent connections.
The catch: CPU-heavy work blocks the loop. A 2-second image resize or a giant JSON.parse freezes every other request on that process. Move it to worker threads, a separate service, or a job queue.
Go uses goroutines (cheap green threads) scheduled over OS threads; Java 21+ has virtual threads. Both let you write blocking-style code that scales.
why: Explains production mysteries like "the whole API stalls when someone exports a big report" and guides what work belongs in request handlers.
trade: To use multiple CPU cores, Node runs several processes (cluster, PM2, or multiple containers). Shared in-memory state then breaks, which is another reason to keep servers stateless.

myth.m: async/await makes code run in parallel.
myth.r: It lets the process do other things while waiting on I/O. Two CPU-bound functions still run one after another on the same thread.

A server handles many users at once. Node.js does it with one main thread: while waiting for the database or network, it serves other requests. This works because most server time is waiting.

The weakness: if one request does heavy calculation, the single thread is busy and every other user waits.
bridge: It is the same event loop as in the browser. A long calculation that freezes your UI will freeze your Node server for all users in the same way.

prod.summary: In production, the event-loop model shows up as tail latency: p99 jumps while CPU on one core is at 100% and the others are idle. Seniors measure event-loop delay, keep CPU-heavy and synchronous work out of request handlers, run one Node process per core (or one per small container), and know which “async” APIs actually run on libuv's small thread pool.
checklist: Event-loop delay is a metric with an alert (for example p99 > 100 ms). Use perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() or your APM's event-loop metric.
No synchronous APIs in request paths: fs.readFileSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync, zlib.gzipSync, or huge JSON.parse/JSON.stringify on multi-MB payloads.
CPU-heavy work (image resize, PDF, big CSV, bcrypt with high cost) runs in worker_threads (a pool such as Piscina), a separate service, or a background job.
Regexes on user input are checked for catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS): one bad pattern blocks the whole process.
Containers are sized for the model: one Node process uses about one core for JS, so a 4-CPU pod with one process wastes three cores. Use more replicas with ~1 CPU each, or cluster mode.
Code that leans on the libuv pool (fs, dns.lookup, async crypto, zlib) is aware that the pool defaults to 4 threads; UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is raised only when measured.
Health checks are cheap, so a busy loop shows up as slow requests, not as a restart storm.
numbers: libuv's thread pool has 4 threads by default; UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE can raise it (maximum 1024). It runs file system work and getaddrinfo (dns.lookup), plus async crypto and zlib in Node.
Java 21 made virtual threads a final feature (JEP 444), so thread-per-request code can scale to very many concurrent requests without async/await.
One synchronous 200 ms task blocks every other request on that process for 200 ms; at 50 requests per second, that is about 10 requests waiting behind it.
failures: p99 latency jumps from 80 ms to 4 s for all routes on one pod, every time someone uploads an avatar.
Image resizing runs on the main thread. Fix: move it to a worker thread pool or a background job; measure event-loop delay to confirm.
Kubernetes restarts Node pods during traffic peaks; logs show liveness probe timeouts but no crashes.

The event loop is blocked long enough that /healthz cannot answer in time. Fix: remove the blocking work; make the liveness probe timeout and failure threshold tolerant; do not make liveness depend on the database.
Requests with an outgoing HTTP call are slow under load, but the remote service is fast.
Many parallel dns.lookup calls (or fs/crypto work) queue behind libuv's 4 pool threads. Fix: reuse connections with keep-alive, cache DNS, and raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE after measuring.
One request with a long, special-character string makes CPU 100% and the process stops answering.
ReDoS: a regex with nested quantifiers backtracks exponentially. Fix: rewrite the regex, limit input length, or use a linear-time engine such as RE2.

qs.s: A Node handler does await Promise.all([hashPassword(a), hashPassword(b)]) where hashPassword uses crypto.pbkdf2Sync inside an async function. Do the two hashes run in parallel?
o: Yes, Promise.all runs them in parallel
No, they run one after another on the main thread and block it
Yes, because pbkdf2 always uses the thread pool
No, Promise.all throws on sync functions
qs.e: Marking a function async does not move its body to another thread. pbkdf2Sync runs on the main thread. The async version crypto.pbkdf2 would run on libuv's pool, which is the fix here.

qs.s: A 4-vCPU Kubernetes pod runs one Node process. Under load, the pod shows 25% CPU, but latency is high. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The pod needs more memory
Kubernetes is throttling the pod
Postgres is overloaded
The single JS thread is saturating one core; the other three are mostly idle
qs.e: One Node process runs JavaScript on one thread, so it can use about one core for JS. 25% of 4 cores is exactly one busy core. Run more processes (cluster or more pods with ~1 CPU each). Throttling would show CPU at the limit, not at 25%.

qs.s: Your monitoring shows event-loop delay p99 of 900 ms, while DB query time is 5 ms. Which change helps most?
o: Add a read replica
Raise the database connection pool from 10 to 50
Find and remove synchronous or CPU-heavy code in handlers (profile with --cpu-prof or clinic)
Enable HTTP/2
qs.e: High loop delay with fast queries means the process is busy computing, not waiting. A CPU profile shows which function blocks. Database changes do not help when the database is not the bottleneck; more connections can even make it worse.

qs.s: A /health request arrives on the same Node process while one /report request is running. How long does /health wait?

code.title: report.ts

o: It answers immediately, because the handler is async.
At most about 30 ms, the time of the database query.
Up to about 900 ms: the loop is synchronous CPU work on the main thread. The await only freed the thread during the query. Better: let the database do it with GROUP BY region.
It fails, because each request runs on its own thread and the pool is full.
qs.e: async functions run synchronously between awaits. The 900 ms loop has no await, so nothing else on that process runs during it. The “30 ms” answer is tempting because it is the only I/O, but I/O is the part that does not block. Moving the aggregation into SQL removes both the CPU work and the 400,000-row transfer.

qs.s: Calculate: 100 logins arrive at once. Each uses async crypto.pbkdf2 taking 100 ms of CPU. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is the default, and the machine has 8 cores. About how long until the last login finishes hashing?
o: About 100 ms
About 2.5 s
About 1.25 s
About 10 s
qs.e: Async pbkdf2 runs on the libuv thread pool, which has 4 threads by default: 100 / 4 = 25 rounds × 100 ms ≈ 2.5 s. With UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 it would be about 1.25 s, and more threads than cores would not help. 10 s would be the fully serial case, which async avoids; 100 ms assumes unlimited parallelism.

The libuv thread pool is too small; raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.
Network latency between the pod and the database.
The main JS thread is CPU-bound (one core at 100%) and blocks the event loop. Profile it (node --cpu-prof or a flame graph) to find the synchronous hot path.
qs.e: Event-loop delay of 1.35 s with one core fully used means JavaScript is busy, not waiting. The database is fast (12 ms) and no client waits for a connection, so the DB answers are ruled out by the data. A small libuv pool shows up as slow fs/dns/crypto calls, not as one core at 100% with a blocked loop.

qs.s: A Go service increments a package-level map[string]int in every HTTP handler. Under load it crashes with fatal error: concurrent map writes. The same logic in Node never crashed. Why?
o: Go runs handlers on many goroutines in parallel across CPU cores, and Go maps are not safe for concurrent writes. Protect the map with a sync.Mutex (or use atomic counters). Node runs your JS on one thread, so two handlers never modify the object at the same moment.
It is a bug in Go's garbage collector.
Node is faster, so the handlers finish before they overlap.
GOMAXPROCS is too low; raise it.
qs.e: In Node, a synchronous statement like counts[k]++ can never be interrupted. Node still has races, but only across await points (read, await, write). Raising GOMAXPROCS is the tempting answer, but more parallelism makes the race more likely, not less.

interview.q: Explain how Node handles 10,000 concurrent connections with one thread. Where does that model break?
answer: Sockets are non-blocking; the OS notifies libuv (epoll/kqueue) when data is ready, and the event loop runs the callback. Waiting costs memory, not a thread.
Some async APIs (fs, dns.lookup, crypto, zlib) run on libuv's thread pool, 4 threads by default.
It breaks on CPU work: anything synchronous (big JSON, loops, sync crypto, ReDoS) stops every connection on that process.
It uses one core for JS; scale with more processes or containers, which requires stateless servers.
Measure it: event-loop delay is the key metric, plus CPU per process.

interview.q: Node, Go or Java with virtual threads for a new API service: how do you choose?
answer: Workload: mostly I/O with little CPU → all three work; heavy CPU per request → Go or Java use all cores in one process.
Team and ecosystem: shared TypeScript with the frontend is a real productivity gain for Node.
Concurrency bugs: Node avoids data races on shared memory (single thread) but has async interleaving bugs; Go/Java need locks or channels.
Operational: Go gives small static binaries and predictable memory; Java has a heavier runtime but strong profiling; Node needs one process per core.
Virtual threads (Java 21) and goroutines let you write blocking-style code that scales, without async/await everywhere.

interview.q: The p99 latency of a Node service spikes at random times. How do you find the cause?
answer: Check event-loop delay and CPU per process at the spike times. High delay + one busy core → blocking JS.
Correlate with routes and payloads: which requests were in flight (traces, slow-request logs with payload sizes).
Profile in production-like conditions: --cpu-prof, a continuous profiler, or flame graphs during load tests.
Look at GC pauses (--trace-gc, heap size near the limit) and libuv pool saturation (slow dns/fs/crypto).
Fix by moving CPU work out (worker pool, job, SQL), streaming large payloads, and limiting input sizes.

one: Work that should not happen inside the user's request (emails, reports, video processing) goes onto a queue for separate worker processes.
an: A dry cleaner gives you a ticket and says "come back Thursday" instead of making you wait at the counter.
how: The request handler writes a job ({type: 'send_receipt', orderId: 42}) to a queue and responds immediately.
Worker processes pull jobs, run them, and mark them done. On failure they retry with backoff; after N failures the job goes to a dead-letter queue for a human to inspect.
Tools: BullMQ / Sidekiq (Redis-backed), Celery, RQ, pg-boss / Graphile Worker (Postgres-backed), SQS, cloud task services. Cron-style scheduled jobs often share the same system.
why: Keeps responses fast, survives third-party outages (the email provider is down → retry later), and lets you scale workers separately from the web tier.
trade: Jobs run at least once, so handlers must be idempotent. You now need to monitor queue depth and failures, or jobs rot silently.

myth.m: I can just do it in a setTimeout after responding.
myth.r: If the process restarts (every deploy does), that work is lost with no retry and no record. A durable queue survives restarts.

Store the upload, enqueue a transcode job, return 202, and notify when done
Use a bigger server

plain:
Some work should not happen while the user waits: sending emails, generating PDFs, processing videos, calling slow external services. Instead, the request puts a “job” in a queue and answers immediately. Separate worker processes take jobs from the queue and do them.

If a job fails, it is retried automatically later.
bridge: It is like replacing a slow await in your click handler with “show ‘We'll email you when it's ready’ and do it later”. The user gets a fast response; the work still happens reliably.

walk.title: Sending a receipt after checkout
steps: The checkout request saves the order, then adds a job: { type: 'send_receipt', orderId: 42 } to the queue. It responds to the user in 100ms.
A worker process picks up the job and calls the email provider.
The email provider is down. The job fails. The queue schedules retries with exponential backoff: 30 seconds, then 60 seconds, then 2 minutes.
On the third try the provider is back; the email is sent and the job is marked done.
If it had failed 5 times, it would go to a “dead-letter” list for a human to look at, instead of being lost.

terms: A list of jobs waiting to be processed.
A process that takes jobs from the queue and runs them.
Trying again with growing waits between attempts.
Where jobs go after too many failures.
insights: Monitor queue length and job age. A silently growing queue is an outage nobody has noticed yet.
Add the job after the database commit, or use an outbox table. A job added inside a transaction that later rolls back runs for an order that does not exist.

prod.summary: In production, a job system is a second application with its own failure modes: jobs that run twice, jobs that disappear, queues that grow silently, and workers killed in the middle of a deploy. Seniors make every job idempotent, configure retries and dead-letter handling explicitly (defaults are often “no retry”), alert on queue age, and make workers shut down cleanly on SIGTERM.
checklist: Retries are configured on purpose. In BullMQ the default is one attempt (no retry); set attempts and backoff (exponential, with jitter).
Every job handler is idempotent: it can run twice (after a crash or a stalled-job recovery) without sending two emails or charging twice.

Jobs carry IDs, not whole objects, and load fresh data when they run. A deterministic jobId (for example receipt-order_42) prevents duplicate enqueues while that job is still stored. BullMQ rejects custom IDs that contain :, and once removeOnComplete deletes the job, the same ID can be added again, so the handler must still be idempotent.
Monitoring covers queue depth, age of the oldest waiting job, failure rate and dead-letter count. Age is the best alert: “oldest job waiting > 5 min”.
Workers handle SIGTERM: stop taking new jobs, finish or release current ones (await worker.close()), then exit before Kubernetes' grace period (30 s by default) ends.
Completed and failed jobs are cleaned up (removeOnComplete/removeOnFail with a count or age), or Redis memory grows forever.
Redis for BullMQ uses maxmemory-policy noeviction; any eviction policy can delete queue keys and lose jobs.
numbers: BullMQ: jobs are tried once unless you set attempts above 1; a worker's job lock lasts 30 seconds by default and is renewed while the job runs, so long CPU-blocking work makes jobs “stall” and run again.
BullMQ's production guide says Redis must use maxmemory-policy noeviction.
AWS SQS: the visibility timeout can be extended, but never beyond 12 hours from when the message was first received.
Kubernetes: default terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30, after which the container is killed with SIGKILL.
failures: Customers get the same email twice, always right after a deploy.

Workers were killed mid-job. The job's lock expired and another worker ran it again after the email was already sent. Fix: graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, and make the job idempotent (record “receipt sent for order 42” before or atomically with sending).
“Job stalled more than allowable limit” errors; the job is a 2-minute PDF render.
CPU-heavy code blocks the worker's event loop, so it cannot renew its lock, and BullMQ assumes the worker died. Fix: run CPU work in a sandboxed processor or worker thread, or split the job.
Emails are delayed by 6 hours, and nobody noticed until customers complained.
The queue grew because one slow job type blocked everything, and only “failures” were monitored. Fix: alert on age of the oldest waiting job; separate queues for fast and slow work.
Redis memory keeps rising and finally hits maxmemory; enqueues fail with OOM command not allowed.
Completed jobs are kept forever (the default), each with its payload. Fix: set removeOnComplete and removeOnFail with an age or count limit, and keep payloads small.

qs.s: A job “charge subscription” fails with a timeout from the payment API. BullMQ retries it 30 seconds later. What must be true for this to be safe?
o: The job passes the same idempotency key to the payment API on every attempt
The retry uses a longer timeout
The job runs on a different worker
The queue uses Redis persistence
qs.e: A timeout does not mean the charge failed; the provider may have completed it. Only an idempotency key per logical charge makes the retry safe. Longer timeouts, other workers and persistence do not prevent a double charge.

qs.s: Which single alert catches the most job-system problems early?
o: Worker CPU above 80%
Number of jobs completed per minute
Redis uptime
Age of the oldest waiting job above a threshold (for example 5 minutes)
qs.e: Age captures every reason work is not getting done: workers down, a stuck job type, not enough capacity, a poison message. Throughput can look normal while one queue starves; CPU and uptime say nothing about waiting work.

qs.s: A developer puts the whole order object (with prices and address) into the job payload. The job runs 10 minutes later after the user changed their address. What is the problem and fix?
o: No problem; payloads are immutable for safety
Redis cannot store objects
The job uses stale data; store only orderId and load fresh data when the job runs
Jobs must run within 1 minute, so delays are the bug
qs.e: Payloads are snapshots. Storing IDs means the job always works with current data and keeps Redis memory small. Snapshots are only right when you intentionally need the value at enqueue time (for example, an audit record).

qs.s: Sometimes the receipt job fails with “order not found”, and sometimes customers receive a receipt for an order that was never saved. Read the code. What is the root cause and the robust fix?

code.title: checkout.ts

o: The job is missing attempts; add retries.

The job is enqueued in Redis before the database transaction commits. A worker can run before the commit, or the transaction can roll back after the job exists. Write the job into an outbox table in the same transaction (or use a Postgres-backed queue) and publish it after commit.
returning() is asynchronous and returns the wrong ID.
The two inserts should run in parallel with Promise.all.
qs.e: Redis and Postgres are two systems, so there is no shared transaction. Moving add() after the transaction is the tempting fix: it solves both symptoms here, but if the process dies between the commit and the add(), the job is lost forever. The outbox makes “order saved” and “job recorded” one atomic write.

qs.s: Calculate: a queue receives 1,200 jobs per minute. Each job takes 2 s, mostly waiting on an external API. You run one worker with concurrency: 10. Is the queue stable?
o: Yes. 10 parallel jobs is plenty for 20 jobs per second.
Yes, as long as Redis is fast enough.
No, but only because Redis is single-threaded.

No. Capacity is 10 slots / 2 s = 5 jobs per second = 300 per minute. The backlog grows by 900 jobs per minute. You need at least 40 concurrent slots, and the external API's rate limit must allow that.
qs.e: Throughput = concurrency / job duration (Little's law). 1,200 per minute is 20 per second, which needs 20 × 2 s = 40 jobs in progress. “10 is plenty” is the tempting answer if you forget that each job occupies its slot for 2 s. Before raising concurrency, check that the external API will not answer with 429s.

qs.s: Video transcode jobs take 3 to 8 minutes. The worker calls await worker.close() on SIGTERM. What happens during every deploy?

code.title: worker-deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: registry.example.com/worker:1.42
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "2"

o: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, the worker stops taking new jobs and waits for running ones, but after 30 s Kubernetes sends SIGKILL and kills it in the middle of the transcode. The job stalls and starts again from zero. Raise the grace period above the longest job, or make jobs resumable in smaller steps.
Kubernetes waits for running jobs to finish before it kills the pod.
BullMQ moves the running jobs to “failed”, and they are lost.
Nothing; Node ignores SIGTERM by default.
qs.e: Graceful shutdown only works if the grace period is longer than the work it waits for. “Kubernetes waits for the jobs” is the tempting belief, but Kubernetes knows nothing about jobs; it waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds and then kills. The lost lock means the job is retried later as stalled, not lost, but all the work so far is wasted. Do not count on that forever: with BullMQ's default maxStalledCount of 1, a job that is killed again on the next deploy is failed with “job stalled more than allowable limit”.

qs.s: Password-reset emails are delayed by 40 minutes whenever marketing sends a 200,000-recipient newsletter. Both use the same emails queue and workers. What is the right fix?
o: Increase attempts on the password-reset jobs.
Use a bigger Redis instance.
Separate queues and worker pools for transactional and bulk work (or priorities with reserved capacity), so bulk work cannot block urgent jobs.
Only send newsletters at night.
qs.e: The reset email waits behind 200,000 newsletter jobs: head-of-line blocking. Separate queues give urgent work its own capacity. Sending newsletters at night is tempting and reduces the pain, but the next bulk job (an export, a migration) causes the same incident. Retries and Redis size do not change the order of the queue.

interview.q: How do you make sure a job is enqueued if and only if the database transaction commits?
answer: The problem: the queue (Redis, SQS) and the database are separate systems, so “commit + enqueue” is a dual write that can half-fail.
Transactional outbox: insert the job/event row in the same transaction; a relay publishes it after commit and marks it sent.
Or use a Postgres-backed queue (pg-boss, Graphile Worker) and insert the job in the same transaction.
The relay delivers at least once, so consumers stay idempotent.
Monitor outbox lag (age of the oldest unsent row).

interview.q: What monitoring and alerts would you set up for a job system?
answer: Age of the oldest waiting job per queue: the single best alert (for example > 5 minutes for transactional jobs).
Queue depth trend, throughput (completed per minute) and failure rate per job type.
Dead-letter count growth, with an owner who reviews it.
Job duration percentiles and stalled-job count (workers killed or blocked).
Store health: Redis memory, eviction policy (noeviction), connection errors.

Who should be paged for dead-letter jobs?

interview.q: How do you design a job that takes 2 hours and must survive deploys?
answer: Split it into smaller idempotent steps or batches (a parent job with child jobs), each a few minutes long.
Checkpoint progress in the database (last processed ID), so a restart continues instead of starting over.
Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, finish the current batch, save the checkpoint, exit within the grace period.
Keep the job lock alive (heartbeat) and keep CPU work off the event loop so the lock can be renewed.
Expose progress to users and operators, and make the job cancellable.
